[2026-15181: lines 1322-1721 of 4520, FR page 47328]
  1322  III. USTR Responses to Significant Comments
  1323  
  1324      In response to the June 5, 2026 FRN, USTR received over 1,600 
  1325  written comments and heard testimony from over 100 witnesses. USTR and 
  1326  the Section 301 Committee reviewed, examined, and considered each 
  1327  comment and the public testimony. USTR responds below to significant 
  1328  issues raised in the public comments and hearings in response to the 
  1329  June 5, 2026 FRN and further explains the Trade Representative's 
  1330  determinations to take appropriate and feasible action under Section 
  1331  301(b) at the specific direction of the President. See 19 U.S.C. 
  1332  2411(b)(2).
  1333  
  1334  A. Response to Comments Regarding Prior Determinations on Actionability
  1335  
  1336      Multiple comments raised arguments taking issue with some or all of 
  1337  the conclusions the Trade Representative reached in his actionability 
  1338  finding and Report in these investigations. These include arguments 
  1339  that the Trade Representative failed to substantiate the existence of 
  1340  unreasonable acts, policies, or practices in each investigation, or 
  1341  that the Trade Representative failed to demonstrate a burden or 
  1342  restriction imposed by the acts, policies, and practices of each 
  1343  economy. With respect to these arguments and other arguments regarding 
  1344  the Trade Representative's earlier findings on actionability, the Trade 
  1345  Representative observes that any such arguments that were appropriately 
  1346  raised during the actionability phase of these investigations were 
  1347  addressed in the June 5, 2026 FRN or the related comprehensive Report. 
  1348  Moreover, the Trade Representative has taken into account all available 
  1349  information regarding the efforts of the investigated economies to 
  1350  impose and effectively enforce forced labor import prohibitions since 
  1351  the issuance of the June 5, 2026 FRN.
  1352  
  1353  B. Comments Regarding the Use of Tariffs and Tariff Rates
  1354  
  1355  1. Responses to Significant Comments Regarding the Appropriateness of 
  1356  the Additional Tariffs To Address the Acts, Policies, and Practices 
  1357  Under Investigation
  1358      A number of comments argued that the additional tariffs proposed in 
  1359  these investigations are not appropriate to achieve the elimination of 
  1360  the unreasonable acts, policies, or practices of each of the 
  1361  investigated economies. These comments argued, among other things, that 
  1362  additional tariffs would be unlikely to significantly lessen the use of 
  1363  forced labor. Other comments argued
  1364  
  1365  [[Page 47329]]
  1366  
  1367  that USTR should undertake diplomatic engagement or engage in technical 
  1368  assistance and capacity building in order to achieve the elimination of 
  1369  the acts, policies, or practices in these investigations.
  1370      With respect to the first argument, consistent with the specific 
  1371  direction of the President, the Trade Representative has determined to 
  1372  impose tariffs as a means to encourage the investigated economies to 
  1373  impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import ban. Further, USTR 
  1374  observes that since the initiation of the investigations and the 
  1375  announcement of the proposed tariff actions, various economies have 
  1376  imposed or are taking steps toward imposing a forced labor import 
  1377  prohibition. This serves to confirm that tariff action can help obtain 
  1378  the elimination of the investigated acts, policies, and practices. 
  1379  While the elimination of forced labor generally is not the aim of these 
  1380  Section 301 investigations, as observed in the Report, the prevalence 
  1381  of forced labor has increased in recent years. Existing efforts to 
  1382  address forced labor have proven inadequate to prevent this increase. 
  1383  As discussed in the Report in these investigations, it is well 
  1384  established that an effectively enforced forced labor import 
  1385  prohibition can lead to the remediation of significant instances of 
  1386  forced labor.
  1387      With respect to technical assistance and capacity building, we 
  1388  observe that such efforts on their own are unlikely to achieve the 
  1389  elimination of the unreasonable acts, policies, and practices. However, 
  1390  where an economy agrees to address the issue of forced labor imports, 
  1391  and seeks assistance to impose or effectively enforce such a 
  1392  prohibition, such activities will be more effective. As discussed 
  1393  above, trade-based measures, particularly tariffs, are encouraging 
  1394  economies to impose or take steps toward imposing a forced labor import 
  1395  prohibition.
  1396      While the Trade Representative has considered the arguments raised 
  1397  in the comments, the Trade Representative disagrees with the comments 
  1398  for the reasons discussed above. Furthermore, because the comments 
  1399  suggested alternative actions that are inconsistent with the specific 
  1400  direction of the President, the Trade Representative cannot accommodate 
  1401  them.
  1402  2. Response to Comments Regarding the Proposed Tariff Rates
  1403      USTR received several types of comments regarding the proposed 
  1404  rates of duty for each investigation. For example, multiple comments 
  1405  questioned whether a 10 or 12.5 percent duty would be significant 
  1406  enough to encourage economies to eliminate the investigated acts, 
  1407  policies, and practices. Some comments argued that the 2.5 percentage 
  1408  point difference between the two rates is not significant enough to 
  1409  encourage economies to eliminate the investigated acts, policies, or 
  1410  practices. Multiple comments argued for certain investigated economies 
  1411  to be excluded from the application of additional duties or be assigned 
  1412  a lower additional rate of duty, including where the economy has 
  1413  domestic laws prohibiting forced labor. Related to these arguments, 
  1414  certain other comments argued that it was not appropriate for economies 
  1415  that have made commitments regarding forced labor in ARTs to receive 
  1416  the same tariff rate as economies with a forced labor import 
  1417  prohibition, or economies that have taken steps towards enforcement of 
  1418  a forced labor import prohibition, or economies with partial regimes 
  1419  with the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor 
  1420  goods. USTR addresses each of these comments in turn.
  1421      With respect to the significance of the rates of duty in these 
  1422  investigations, including the differential of 2.5 percentage points, 
  1423  the Trade Representative has determined that the rate for each economy 
  1424  is appropriate to obtain the elimination of that economy's acts, 
  1425  policies, and practices at this time. The Trade Representative 
  1426  considers that a lower rate of duty would not be appropriate to obtain 
  1427  the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices, at this time. The 
  1428  specific action and level of duty that will obtain the elimination of 
  1429  an act, policy, or practice is a matter of judgment, to be exercised by 
  1430  the Trade Representative, subject to any specific direction of the 
  1431  President. Information available indicates that these tariff rates and 
  1432  the differential between them are significant enough to spur action by 
  1433  investigated economies. Since the publication of the proposed actions 
  1434  in these investigations, a number of economies have either imposed 
  1435  forced labor import prohibitions, or undertaken a commitment to impose 
  1436  a forced labor import prohibition as part of an ART. Other economies 
  1437  have informed USTR that they are in the process of developing such 
  1438  measures. Accordingly, the rates and the differential between them have 
  1439  been successful in encouraging investigated economies to take steps 
  1440  toward eliminating the investigated acts, policies, and practices.
  1441      With respect to excluding economies or providing a lower rate of 
  1442  duty based on those economies' efforts to address forced labor within 
  1443  their jurisdictions, such as the ratification of International Labor 
  1444  Organization (ILO) conventions or domestic enforcement efforts related 
  1445  to forced labor, doing so would not achieve the elimination of the 
  1446  investigated acts, policies, and practices. The Trade Representative 
  1447  applauds the efforts of our trading partners to eliminate forced labor 
  1448  within their jurisdictions; however, as discussed in our June 5, 2026 
  1449  FRN and the related Report, these efforts are not pertinent to the 
  1450  elimination of the acts, policies, and practices that are the subject 
  1451  of these investigations.
  1452      With respect to excluding or providing a lower rate to economies 
  1453  that are in the process of developing forced labor import prohibitions, 
  1454  the mere development or proposal of a measure to prohibit the 
  1455  importation of forced labor goods, absent adoption of such measure, is 
  1456  insufficient to address the acts, policies, and practices that are the 
  1457  subject of these investigations. The development or proposal of such 
  1458  measures alone provides no guarantee that a forced labor import 
  1459  prohibition will be adopted and effectively enforced. Further, this is 
  1460  distinct from circumstances where an economy has taken on a concrete 
  1461  obligation to prohibit the importation of goods. Certain comments 
  1462  contend that the Trade Representative should assign different rates of 
  1463  duty to each of the following groups of economies: (1) those that have 
  1464  imposed forced labor import prohibitions; (2) those that made 
  1465  commitments regarding forced labor in an ART or other similar 
  1466  agreement; and (3) those that have imposed a partial regime with the 
  1467  effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods. In 
  1468  the Trade Representative's judgment, imposing distinct tariff rates on 
  1469  each of these groups at this time would hinder the ability of the Trade 
  1470  Representative to achieve the elimination of the investigated acts, 
  1471  policies, and practices. The Trade Representative's determination to 
  1472  apply a lower rate of duty to each economy meeting these criteria 
  1473  acknowledges significant steps such economies are taking toward 
  1474  imposing and effectively enforcing forced labor import prohibitions.
  1475      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1476  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees, and consistent 
  1477  with the specific direction of the President, the Trade Representative 
  1478  has determined that it is appropriate to impose tariffs of 10 percent 
  1479  or 10 percent net of MFN duties, based on whether an economy has 
  1480  imposed a
  1481  
  1482  [[Page 47330]]
  1483  
  1484  forced labor import prohibition, has undertaken commitments in an ART 
  1485  regarding forced labor import prohibition, or has imposed a partial 
  1486  regime with the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced 
  1487  labor goods, and has determined that it is appropriate to impose 
  1488  tariffs of 12.5 percent or 12.5 percent net of MFN duties for each 
  1489  other investigated economy. In the Trade Representative's judgment, 
  1490  imposing an economy-wide rate of zero or lower than 10 percent on 
  1491  economies that have entered into an ART without implementing a forced 
  1492  labor import prohibition, or on economies that have imposed a 
  1493  prohibition but do not yet effectively implement such prohibition, 
  1494  would be ineffective in encouraging the elimination of the acts, 
  1495  policies, and practices under investigation. While the Trade 
  1496  Representative has considered the arguments raised in the comments, the 
  1497  Trade Representative disagrees with the comments for the reasons 
  1498  discussed above. Furthermore, because the comments suggested 
  1499  alternative actions that are inconsistent with the specific direction 
  1500  of the President, the Trade Representative cannot accommodate them.
  1501  3. Response to Comments Urging Lower Tariff Rates in Investigations of 
  1502  Economies With Perceived Low-Risk Supply
  1503      Multiple comments suggested that the Trade Representative should 
  1504  impose a lower or zero tariff rate on economies with export industries 
  1505  that have a low-risk of forced labor in their supply chains. For 
  1506  example, certain commenters argued that where investigated economies 
  1507  export products to major U.S. retailers with their own supply chain due 
  1508  diligence procedures, additional tariffs on such products would be 
  1509  ineffective in bringing about the elimination of the investigated acts, 
  1510  policies, and practices. These comments misunderstand the aims of the 
  1511  investigations and the use of tariffs as leverage.
  1512      As demonstrated throughout the investigations, including in the 
  1513  Report, the investigations are broader than any particular industry or 
  1514  supply chain. The aim of each investigation is to encourage that 
  1515  economy to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import 
  1516  prohibition. As already seen in certain investigations to date, tariffs 
  1517  have proved to be an effective point of leverage to encourage the 
  1518  elimination of the investigated acts, policies, and practices. Even 
  1519  accepting these arguments at face value, it does not follow that U.S. 
  1520  products do not compete in those economies against other imports 
  1521  manufactured with forced labor, or that other exports from those 
  1522  economies (i.e., those not subject to supply chain due diligence 
  1523  procedures) are not manufactured with imported inputs made with forced 
  1524  labor. While the Trade Representative has considered the arguments 
  1525  raised in the comments, the Trade Representative disagrees with the 
  1526  comments for the reasons discussed above. Furthermore, because the 
  1527  comments suggested alternative actions that are inconsistent with the 
  1528  specific direction of the President, the Trade Representative cannot 
  1529  accommodate them.
  1530  
  1531  C. Discussion of Comments on Proposed Product Exemptions
  1532  
  1533      USTR received a variety of comments on the proposed exemption list, 
  1534  including support for the products proposed for exemption and requests 
  1535  to remove certain products from the proposed exemption list. 
  1536  Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1537  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees and in 
  1538  accordance with the specific direction of the President, the Trade 
  1539  Representative has determined to exempt all of the products proposed 
  1540  for exemption in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN, except the non-
  1541  pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products. Other than 
  1542  the products with non-pharmaceutical applications, as discussed below, 
  1543  the Trade Representative determined not to remove additional products 
  1544  from the exemption list. The Trade Representative determined to exempt 
  1545  certain additional products not included in the proposed exemptions in 
  1546  Annex A to June 5, 2026 FRN.
  1547  1. Support for Keeping Products on the Proposed Exemption List
  1548      USTR received a number of comments expressing support for 
  1549  maintaining certain proposed exemptions. Comments supported the 
  1550  exemption of coffee, mineral tars, certain copper products, iron 
  1551  oxides, coke, aluminum oxide, and coconut products. Other comments 
  1552  expressed support for maintaining the proposed exemptions from Section 
  1553  301 tariffs for products that are subject to Section 232 tariffs. 
  1554  Commenters generally noted that these products are raw materials with 
  1555  limited-to-no availability from domestic sources or cannot be grown or 
  1556  produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the United 
  1557  States or obtained from other sources.
  1558      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1559  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1560  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1561  Representative has determined not to remove products other than the 
  1562  non-pharmaceutical applications of certain products from the proposed 
  1563  exemption list, as the remaining products in the proposed exemption 
  1564  list constitute: (1) raw materials that if subject to the proposed 
  1565  additional tariffs could lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; 
  1566  (2) products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to 
  1567  the proposed additional tariffs; (3) products that cannot be grown or 
  1568  produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the United 
  1569  States or obtained from other sources; or (4) products for which 
  1570  tariffs may not contribute substantially to the elimination of the 
  1571  acts, policies, and practices found to be actionable.
  1572  2. Determination To Remove Certain Products From the Proposed Exemption 
  1573  List
  1574      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  1575  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  1576  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  1577  Representative has determined to limit the exemption for certain 
  1578  chemicals and chemical products to their pharmaceutical applications. 
  1579  Certain comments noted the health-related applications of products 
  1580  proposed for exemptions and stated that certain ingredients that 
  1581  support U.S. manufacturing of healthcare products are not available in 
  1582  the United States in sufficient quantities to meet domestic demand. 
  1583  Some commenters also requested that these product exemptions be limited 
  1584  to their pharmaceutical applications due to competition with domestic 
  1585  production. Limiting exemptions for these proposed chemical products to 
  1586  their pharmaceutical applications is consistent with the proposal in 
  1587  the June 5, 2026 FRN because an exemption for all applications is 
  1588  broader than necessary to cover goods that have limited availability 
  1589  outside of the investigated economies.
  1590  3. Comments Requesting the Removal of Additional Products From 
  1591  Exemption List
  1592      Some commenters requested that USTR remove other products from the 
  1593  proposed exemption list or otherwise advocated for narrowly tailored 
  1594  exemptions. Industries or products for which commenters expressed
  1595  
  1596  [[Page 47331]]
  1597  
  1598  opposition to proposed exemptions include beef, avocados, paprika and 
  1599  paprika products, lithium hexafluorophosphate, and forgings and 
  1600  articles containing forgings.
  1601      Commenters suggested, for example, that beef imported from certain 
  1602  economies is linked to certain acts, policies, and practices found 
  1603  actionable in these investigations, and that exempting these products 
  1604  would benefit foreign exporters of beef produced with forced labor at 
  1605  the expense of the American cattle producer. Similarly, commenters 
  1606  suggested that paprika and paprika derived products, lithium 
  1607  hexafluorophosphate, and certain chemicals used in the production of 
  1608  pesticides are imported from certain economies linked to certain acts, 
  1609  policies, and practices found actionable in these investigations.
  1610      Additionally, commenters suggested that imports of these products 
  1611  are available from domestic sources and are putting pressure on 
  1612  domestic producers. With respect to paprika and paprika derived 
  1613  products, commenters suggested that imports have caused market 
  1614  disruptions, preventing U.S. production of these products. 
  1615  Additionally, comments reported that imports of lithium 
  1616  hexafluorophosphate and certain chemicals used in the production of 
  1617  pesticides have inhibited U.S. production of these products. Commenters 
  1618  pointed to recent and anticipated expansion in U.S. production 
  1619  capabilities, and suggested that imposing tariffs on these products 
  1620  could support investment and employment in domestic production. With 
  1621  respect to forgings and articles containing forgings, commenters 
  1622  suggested that these products are readily available from domestic 
  1623  sources, at reasonable prices, in sufficient quantities and that 
  1624  subjecting imports of these products to tariffs could support

  1893  E. Determination Not To Exempt Additional Products and Response to 
  1894  Comments
  1895  
  1896      USTR received numerous comments that requested that additional 
  1897  products be added to the exemption list and exempted from tariffs. 
  1898  These comments covered products in a wide range of industries. Most 
  1899  comments that requested that particular products be added to the 
  1900  exemption list based their request on six arguments. These included: 
  1901  (1) requested products have limited or no availability from U.S. 
  1902  source; (2) additional tariffs would increase costs for producers and 
  1903  consumers; (3) tariffs are a competitive disadvantage for U.S. 
  1904  businesses; (4) products requested for exemption are unrelated to the 
  1905  acts, policies, and practices investigated; (5) tariffs would not shift 
  1906  production to the United States; and (6) the tariffs would cause 
  1907  economy-wide disruptions. These six arguments are discussed below, 
  1908  followed by a response to those arguments.
  1909      Products have limited or no availability from U.S. sources. A large 
  1910  number of comments requested the exemption of products due to limited 
  1911  or no availability from domestic sources. These products included 
  1912  medical devices, decorations, frozen seafood, beads, hats, refined 
  1913  lead, olive oil, packaging products, travel products, and sporting 
  1914  goods.
  1915      Several comments noted that domestic producers supplied only a 
  1916  small portion of U.S. demand or were unable to meet all of domestic 
  1917  demand. Comments also noted that their products were not available from 
  1918  domestic sources at reasonable prices or domestic production was not 
  1919  commercially viable, as no domestic producer has the production 
  1920  capacity, specialized equipment, technical expertise, or quality 
  1921  systems necessary to supply the domestic market. Due to the lack of 
  1922  domestic sources, some comments noted that companies would be forced to 
  1923  curtail their business. Additionally, some comments noted that because 
  1924  so many economies would be covered by the tariffs, it would not be 
  1925  possible to shift production to economies not subject to the tariffs 
  1926  and doing so would require significant time and investment.
  1927      Increased costs. Numerous comments reported that the tariffs would 
  1928  result in increased costs to U.S. companies and consumers. These 
  1929  comments came from a range of industries, including: sugar, travel 
  1930  bags, agricultural packaging products, food products, parts and 
  1931  accessories for inkjet printing, and auto parts.
  1932      Comments noted that due to limited domestic availability, costs 
  1933  would increase for U.S. supply chains, including for U.S. food and U.S. 
  1934  manufacturing. Comments noted increasing production costs would result 
  1935  in a reduction in U.S. investment and the funds necessary to create 
  1936  conditions of fair trade, including responsible labor practices. 
  1937  Commenters also suggested that the increased costs would impact 
  1938  retailers, small businesses, and consumers. A comment regarding parts 
  1939  and accessories for inkjet printing systems reported that the tariffs 
  1940  would increase operating and maintenance costs for U.S. companies, 
  1941  extend repair times, disrupt production, and reduce the competitiveness 
  1942  of U.S. manufacturers. Similarly, a comment on auto parts noted that as 
  1943  a result of the tariffs, U.S. distributors, repair shops, and consumers 
  1944  would face higher prices, reduced product availability, and diminished 
  1945  competitiveness in the aftermarket supply chain.
  1946      Competitive disadvantage for U.S. businesses. Comments from a 
  1947  variety of industries noted that tariffs put products produced in the 
  1948  United States at a competitive disadvantage domestically and in 
  1949  international markets. With respect to agricultural and horticultural
  1950  
  1951  [[Page 47334]]
  1952  
  1953  products, for example, commenters noted that they rely upon imports to 
  1954  operate efficiently and remain competitive. Similarly, a comment 
  1955  regarding imports of goose down used in domestic production noted that 
  1956  tariffs on the raw materials will increase costs on domestic 
  1957  manufacturing, making their products less accessible to U.S. consumers. 
  1958  A global producer of electric bicycles that assembles bicycles in the 
  1959  United States using certain imported parts reported that the tariffs 
  1960  will make the company's U.S. subsidiary its most expensive production 
  1961  facility. A commenter seeking an exemption for powersports vehicles 
  1962  reported that it relies on certain imported inputs and that a portion 
  1963  of its domestic manufacturing is supported by exports. Similarly, a 
  1964  comment regarding loudspeakers noted that domestic producers that rely 
  1965  on imported components are disadvantaged when selling in international 
  1966  markets when those components are subject to increased tariffs.
  1967      Products unrelated to the acts, policies, and practices 
  1968  investigated. Many comments argued that the tariffs should be narrowly 
  1969  tailored to specific products linked to forced labor. These comments 
  1970  noted that the products for which they requested exemption from tariffs 
  1971  were not related to the acts, policies, and practices found actionable 
  1972  in these investigations. Those products include: historical coins; 
  1973  radiators and other parts and accessories for motor vehicles; manuka 
  1974  honey; artificial floral, greenery, and seasonal decorative products; 
  1975  various electrical and lighting products; canned olives; and purified 
  1976  isophthalic acid. The comments emphasized that certain imports and 
  1977  sectors have no connection to forced labor. For example, regarding 
  1978  historical coins, a comment noted that the importation of those goods 
  1979  has no connection to forced labor because they were typically produced 
  1980  by skilled laborers or long ago.
  1981      Tariffs would not shift production to the United States. Some 
  1982  comments, such as those related to hydraulic log splitters, women's 
  1983  outerwear and insulated garments, stainless steel insulated drinkware, 
  1984  outer shell covers for pets, cyanate ester resins, crayons, salmon, and 
  1985  finished bovine upholstery leather argued that tariffs should not be 
  1986  applied to their products, as the tariffs would not shift production to 
  1987  the United States. Many of these comments argued that for a variety of 
  1988  reasons, production in the United States is not feasible.
  1989      Tariffs would cause economy-wide disruptions. Some comments, such 
  1990  as those related to toys and DL-methionine, suggested that tariffs 
  1991  would cause economy-wide disruptions. With respect to DL-methionine, 
  1992  commenters noted that tariffs risk serious disruption to the U.S. 
  1993  economy, including U.S. poultry, dairy, beef, and swine producers that 
  1994  depend on imports of that essential nutrient for livestock, and that 
  1995  the additional tariff is likely to disrupt the feed supply chain for 
  1996  U.S. livestock producers.
  1997      The President has directed the Trade Representative to impose 
  1998  tariffs on all goods of the 60 investigated economies, with certain 
  1999  exemptions. Exemptions directed by the President are limited to: (1) 
  2000  raw materials that if subject to the proposed additional tariffs could 
  2001  lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; (2) products that could 
  2002  cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to the proposed additional 
  2003  tariffs; (3) products that cannot be grown or produced in sufficient 
  2004  quantities or at reasonable prices in the United States or obtained 
  2005  from other sources; (4) products for which tariffs may not contribute 
  2006  substantially to the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices 
  2007  found to be actionable; or (5) products that if exempted from these 
  2008  tariffs would encourage economies that have made commitments to the 
  2009  United States regarding forced labor import prohibitions to implement 
  2010  those commitments or to enact and effectively enforce a forced labor 
  2011  import prohibition.
  2012      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  2013  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  2014  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  2015  Representative has determined that the goods above and other goods do 
  2016  not warrant exemption. With respect to the large number of the comments 
  2017  requesting exemption based on availability, most were not raw 
  2018  materials. Rather, most requests were for inputs or consumer goods. 
  2019  While some inputs and consumer goods may have limited or no 
  2020  availability from U.S. sources, those products should remain generally 
  2021  available and will not cause economy-wide disruptions if subjected to 
  2022  additional tariffs. Regarding tariffs resulting in increased costs, it 
  2023  is possible that costs will increase, but a number of factors may 
  2024  affect costs, and increased costs for a particular company or in a 
  2025  particular sector are unlikely to cause economy-wide disruptions. With 
  2026  respect to the argument that tariffs may result in a competitive 
  2027  disadvantage to certain domestic producers, a competitive disadvantage 
  2028  does not indicate unavailability of domestic supply or that products 
  2029  cannot be produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in 
  2030  the United States. Moreover, many inputs, including auto parts already 
  2031  subject to Section 232 tariffs, are exempt from additional tariffs 
  2032  pursuant to this action.
  2033      With respect to the comments that argued that the tariffs should be 
  2034  narrowly tailored to specific products linked to forced labor, imposing 
  2035  tariffs on imports can create greater leverage to obtain the 
  2036  elimination of the investigated acts, policies, and practices, and as 
  2037  described above, Section 301(c)(3)(B) of the Trade Act authorizes the 
  2038  Trade Representative to take action against any goods or economic 
  2039  sector of the foreign country concerned regardless of whether or not 
  2040  such goods or economic sector are involved in the act, policy, or 
  2041  practice subject to investigation. Regarding comments that argued that 
  2042  the tariffs would not shift production to the United States, the goal 
  2043  of the tariff action is not to create domestic production, but to 
  2044  obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, or practices found to be 
  2045  actionable. Finally, with respect to the comments that argued that the 
  2046  tariffs would cause economy-wide disruptions, the comments fail to 
  2047  demonstrate how tariffs on these products would cause economy-wide 
  2048  disruptions, particularly with maximum tariffs of 12.5 percent.
  2049      While the Trade Representative has considered the arguments raised 
  2050  in the comments, the Trade Representative disagrees with the comments 
  2051  for the reasons discussed above. Furthermore, because the comments 
  2052  suggested alternative actions that are inconsistent with the specific 
  2053  direction of the President, the Trade Representative cannot accommodate 
  2054  them.

  2080  G. Response to Comments Suggesting Action Other Than Tariffs
  2081  
  2082      Certain comments recommended the Trade Representative establish an 
  2083  exclusion process, or engage in a periodic review of the actions taken 
  2084  in these investigations. As discussed above, the President directed the 
  2085  imposition of tariffs in each investigation on all products of that 
  2086  economy, with exemptions for certain goods, finding that alternatives

   286  IV. Proposed Actions To Be Taken in the Investigations
   287  
   288      Section 301(b) of the Trade Act provides that upon determining that 
   289  the acts, policies, and practices under investigation are actionable 
   290  and that action is appropriate, the Trade Representative shall take all 
   291  appropriate and feasible action authorized under section 301(c), 
   292  subject to the specific direction, if any, of the President regarding 
   293  such action, and all other appropriate and feasible action within the 
   294  power of the President, that the President may direct the Trade 
   295  Representative to take under section 301(b), to obtain the elimination 
   296  of that act, policy, or practice.
   297      Section 301(c) of the Trade Act authorizes the Trade Representative 
   298  to take certain actions for purposes of carrying out the provisions of 
   299  Section 301(b). Among others, Section 301(c)(1)(B) authorizes the Trade 
   300  Representative to ``impose duties or other import restrictions'' on the 
   301  goods of the foreign country subject to the investigation.
   302      Pursuant to Sections 301(b) and (c), the Trade Representative 
   303  proposes to determine that action is appropriate and that appropriate 
   304  action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices 
   305  would include the imposition of ad valorem duties on all products of 
   306  the 60 economies subject to investigations, except as provided in Annex 
   307  A to this Notice. The proposed exemptions in Annex A include all 
   308  articles and parts currently subject to section 232 tariffs and raw 
   309  materials that if subject to the proposed additional tariffs could lead 
   310  to the unavailability of domestic supply. Annex A also includes 
   311  products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to the 
   312  proposed additional tariffs and certain products that cannot be grown 
   313  or produced in sufficient quantities in the United States or obtained 
   314  from other sources. The proposed exemptions include informational 
   315  materials (e.g., books), donations, and accompanied baggage. Finally, 
   316  the proposed exemptions include articles for which additional tariffs 
   317  may not contribute substantially to the elimination of the investigated 
   318  acts, policies, and practices described above.
   319      For economies that impose a forced labor import prohibition--
   320  Canada, Ecuador, the European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, and Pakistan; 
   321  for economies that have undertaken commitments in their respective 
   322  Agreements on Reciprocal Trade regarding forced labor import 
   323  prohibitions--Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, 
   324  Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Taiwan; and economies that have 
   325  imposed a partial regime with the effect of preventing the importation 
   326  of certain forced labor goods--the United Kingdom; the Trade 
   327  Representative proposes additional duties of 10% for products of these 
   328  economies. For all other economies that have failed to impose and 
   329  effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition, the Trade 
   330  Representative proposes 12.5% as the rate of additional duties.
   331      The Trade Representative also proposes a textile mechanism that 
   332  would allow for a certain volume of apparel and textile imports to 
   333  enter the United States at a reduced Section 301 tariff rate. Under 
   334  such a textile mechanism, the volume of reduced-duty imports from 
   335  certain trading partners would be equivalent to the quantity of exports 
   336  of textiles (e.g., U.S. produced man-made and cotton fiber textile 
   337  inputs) from the United States to that trading partner. A certain 
   338  volume of apparel and textile imports would also be allowed to enter 
   339  the United States at the reduced Section 301 rate based on the volume 
   340  of U.S. cotton and cotton products a trading partner imports from the 
   341  United States during a certain period of time.
   342  
   343  V. Response to Significant Comments
   344  
   345      USTR responds below to significant issues raised in the public 
   346  comments and hearings in response to the March 17, 2026, Federal 
   347  Register notice.
   348  
   349  Response to Significant Comments Raising Legal Arguments Regarding 
   350  Findings of ``Unreasonableness''
   351  
   352      Multiple comments raised threshold arguments that the Trade 
   353  Representative should not find that the failure of an economy to impose 
   354  and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods 
   355  produced with forced labor is unreasonable where: (1) an economy has 
   356  domestic laws prohibiting forced labor; (2) where no international 
   357  standards exists which provide an affirmative obligation on economies 
   358  to impose a forced labor import prohibition; or (3) where an economy 
   359  has otherwise made commitments to the United States with respect to 
   360  imposing and/or enforcing a forced labor import prohibition. This 
   361  section takes each of these arguments in turn.
   362      With respect to the first argument, and as explained in the Report 
   363  and above, solely prohibiting forced labor domestically is unreasonable 
   364  because it fails to discipline the influx of forced labor goods or to 
   365  prevent domestic producers from using forced labor inputs. Thus, while 
   366  an economy may have taken steps to ensure that the condition of forced 
   367  labor is extinguished within its borders, the economy nevertheless 
   368  permits market conditions where imported forced labor goods have a 
   369  competitive advantage over U.S. goods imported into their economy.
   370      In response to the second argument, USTR notes the Section 301 
   371  statute,
   372  
   373  [[Page 34275]]
   374  
   375  which governs these investigations, does not require the existence of 
   376  international standards discipling specific conduct as a prerequisite 
   377  to a finding of an unreasonable act, policy, or practice under Section 
   378  301(b) of the Trade Act. As explained in the Report, the definition of 
   379  unreasonable acts, policies, and practices in Section 301(d) 
   380  contemplates circumstances where, as here, acts, policies, and 
   381  practices of a foreign country may not be inconsistent with or violate 
   382  the international legal rights of the United States, but are 
   383  nevertheless unfair. Thus, the statutory structure of Section 301 
   384  contemplates that the Trade Representative may find unreasonable 
   385  conduct on the part of a trading partner even in the absence of 
   386  international standards or obligations.
   387      Third, some comments argued that where an economy has made 
   388  commitments to the United States regarding forced labor import 
   389  prohibitions, including through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, the 
   390  Trade Representative is without basis to find that same economy's 
   391  failure to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import 
   392  prohibition is unreasonable. USTR applauds Argentina, Bangladesh, 
   393  Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and 
   394  Taiwan, which have undertaken commitments regarding a forced labor 
   395  import prohibition. However, commitments to take action in the future 
   396  is distinct from forbidding legally the importation of forced labor 
   397  goods, and effectively enforcing such prohibition. Until such time as 
   398  the commitment is implemented, U.S. products will continue to compete 
   399  against forced labor products that have a competitive advantage in 
   400  global markets which, among other reasons explained in the Report, is 
   401  unreasonable.
   402      The Trade Representative fully expects economies that have 
   403  undertaken commitments related to prohibiting the importation of forced 
   404  labor goods to abide by those commitments. Accordingly, the Trade 
   405  Representative proposes that the additional duty rate to be applied in 
   406  the investigations take into account whether an economy has undertaken 
   407  such commitments.
   408  
   409  Response to Significant Comments Regarding Actions To Be Taken in the 
   410  Investigations
   411  
   412      A number of comments responded on potential responsive action by 
   413  the Trade Representative. These comments recommended that the Trade 
   414  Representative engage in multilateral negotiations, including at the 
   415  ILO, to encourage economies to impose a forced labor import prohibition 
   416  rather than take ``punitive measures,'' and to provide capacity 
   417  building and technical assistance, especially to developing economies, 
   418  to encourage effective enforcement of such a prohibition.
   419      The Trade Representative proposes that taking an action is 
   420  appropriate, and that action includes the imposition of additional 
   421  duties on products of the investigated economies, in order to obtain 
   422  the elimination of the investigated acts, policies, or practices. 
   423  However, the Trade Representative will continue to consider these 
   424  comments in conjunction with any action that might be taken with

**Evaluating tool budget**

I'm noticing that the tool budget seems a bit misleading with its resets. The actual remaining amount should be 93, but we started with a 49k token budget and had an initial count of 62. Now, the model shows 51, which at least seems sufficient for now. However, I need to gather more documents for Q15. Maybe I should approach the search in a parallel, targeted manner to be more efficient.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

    56                  Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026
    57  
    58                  
    59  Further Adjusting the Tariff Regimes for Imports 
    60                  of Aluminum, Steel, and Copper Into the United States
    61  
    62                  By the President of the United States of America
    63  
    64                  A Proclamation
    65  
    66                  1. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    67                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), as 
    68                  amended; Proclamation 9705 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    69                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), as amended; 
    70                  and Proclamation 10962 of July 30, 2025 (Adjusting 
    71                  Imports of Copper Into the United States), as amended, 
    72                  I found, under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act 
    73                  of 1962, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1862 (section 232), that 
    74                  aluminum, steel, and copper are being imported into the 
    75                  United States in such quantities or under such 
    76                  circumstances as to threaten to impair the national 
    77                  security of the United States and took action under 
    78                  section 232 to adjust imports of aluminum, steel, and 
    79                  copper articles and their derivative articles 
    80                  (collectively, metal products) so that such imports 
    81                  will not threaten to impair the national security. 
    82                  Specifically, to address the national security threats 
    83                  found in Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and 
    84                  Proclamation 10962, I established tariff regimes, which 
    85                  included imposing additional ad valorem duties on 
    86                  certain imports of metal products.
    87  
    88                  2. In Proclamation 11021 of April 2, 2026 
    89                  (Strengthening Actions Taken To Adjust Imports of 
    90                  Aluminum, Steel, and Copper Into the United States), I 
    91                  modified the tariff regimes established under section 
    92                  232 for imports of metal products to more effectively 
    93                  address the national security threats found in 
    94                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 
    95                  10962. In particular, I imposed an ad valorem duty of 
    96                  50 percent on products made of those metals; an ad 
    97                  valorem duty of 25 percent on derivative products that 
    98                  tend to be predominately composed of those metals; and 
    99                  a temporarily-reduced ad valorem duty of 15 percent on 
   100                  a subset of derivative products, namely fixed 
   101                  industrial machinery and power equipment.
   102  
   103                  3. Based on the Secretary of Commerce's (Secretary) 
   104                  monitoring and consultation with other senior 
   105                  officials, among other things, the Secretary has 
   106                  provided me information, opinions, and recommendations 
   107                  regarding the tariff regimes imposed in Proclamation 
   108                  9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; and 
   109                  Proclamation 10962, as amended, and the national 
   110                  security threats found in those proclamations. Among 
   111                  other things, the Secretary has informed me that recent 
   112                  circumstances have affected and are affecting domestic 
   113                  industries that use agricultural equipment, industrial 
   114                  equipment and machinery, and other related products. 
   115                  Many products in these categories are treated as 
   116                  derivative articles of aluminum or steel because they 
   117                  tend to be predominantly composed of aluminum or steel. 
   118                  These products also serve an important role in 
   119                  productive domestic economic activity. For example, 
   120                  American farmers use agricultural equipment to produce 
   121                  the food upon which our Nation relies; construction 
   122                  equipment is essential for the continued 
   123                  reindustrialization of our Nation; and material-
   124                  handling equipment enables industrial logistics and 
   125                  factory operations.
   126  
   127                  4. To account for these circumstances, the Secretary 
   128                  recommended that I modify the tariffs imposed on these 
   129                  products pursuant to Proclamation 9704, as amended, and 
   130                  Proclamation 9705, as amended. In particular, the 
   131                  Secretary recommended that I expand the category of 
   132                  derivative products
   133  
   134  [[Page 34086]]
   135  
   136                  subject to the temporarily-reduced 15 percent ad 
   137                  valorem duty to include agricultural equipment and 
   138                  certain heating, ventilation, and air conditioning 
   139                  (HVAC) systems and components that are predominately 
   140                  for residential use, which are currently treated as 
   141                  aluminum or steel derivative products. The Secretary 
   142                  also recommended that I temporarily modify the tariffs 
   143                  imposed on mobile industrial equipment and machinery to 
   144                  support the American businesses and factories that use 
   145                  these products.
   146  
   147                  5. In addition, the Secretary has recommended that I 
   148                  include two types of aluminum and steel products 
   149                  (aluminum lithographic plates and steel racks) that are 
   150                  not currently subject to aluminum and steel tariffs 
   151                  within the product coverage of Proclamation 11021, to 
   152                  ensure that they are subject to the appropriate tariffs 
   153                  for aluminum and steel derivative products and to 
   154                  ensure that the purpose of the tariff regimes to 
   155                  address the national security threats found in 
   156                  Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9705 are not 
   157                  undermined. The Secretary also recommended that I 
   158                  modify the threshold for imported products to qualify 
   159                  as made ``entirely'' from American aluminum, steel, or 
   160                  copper, as that term is used in Proclamation 11021.
   161  
   162                  6. After considering the current information, opinions, 
   163                  and recommendations newly provided by the Secretary; 
   164                  the factors in section 232 (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)); the 
   165                  need to address the national security threats found in 
   166                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 
   167                  10962; and other relevant factors and information, I 
   168                  determine that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   169                  modify, as further described below, the tariff regimes 
   170                  for metal products imposed in Proclamation 9704, as 
   171                  amended, Proclamation 9705, as amended, and 
   172                  Proclamation 10962, as amended.
   173  
   174                  7. I determine that agricultural equipment and certain 
   175                  HVAC systems and components that are predominantly for 
   176                  residential use shall be included in the category of 
   177                  derivative products subject to the temporarily-reduced 
   178                  15 percent ad valorem duty under Proclamation 11021. In 
   179                  my judgment, this modification appropriately accounts 
   180                  for these products' roles in productive economic 
   181                  activity in the United States and accounts for recent 
   182                  circumstances affecting the relevant industries and 
   183                  services that use these products, while also enabling 
   184                  the tariff regimes to continue effectively addressing 
   185                  the national security threats found in Proclamation 
   186                  9704 and Proclamation 9705.
   187  
   188                  8. I determine that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   189                  temporarily modify the tariffs imposed on mobile 
   190                  industrial equipment and machinery, as detailed below. 
   191                  In my judgment, this temporary modification 
   192                  appropriately accounts for these products' roles in 
   193                  productive economic activity in the United States and 
   194                  accounts for recent circumstances affecting the 
   195                  relevant industries and services that use these 
   196                  products, while also allowing the tariff regimes to 
   197                  continue effectively addressing the national security 
   198                  threats found in Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 
   199                  9705.
   200  
   201                  9. I determine that aluminum lithographic plates and 
   202                  steel racks constitute aluminum and steel derivative 
   203                  products that should be subject to the applicable 
   204                  derivative tariff under Proclamation 11021. In my 
   205                  judgment, subjecting these products to the derivative 
   206                  tariff in Proclamation 11021 will ensure that the 
   207                  tariffs on metal products are not circumvented and that 
   208                  the purpose of the actions to address the national 
   209                  security threats found in Proclamation 9704 and 
   210                  Proclamation 9705 is not undermined.
   211  
   212                  10. I determine that it is appropriate to modify the 
   213                  threshold for imported products to qualify as made 
   214                  ``entirely'' from American aluminum, steel, or copper, 
   215                  as that term is used in Proclamation 11021. The current 
   216                  threshold of 95 percent shall be modified to 85 
   217                  percent. In my judgment, this modification will 
   218                  incentivize increased use of American aluminum, steel, 
   219                  and copper in downstream derivative products and 
   220                  further the purpose of the actions to address the 
   221                  national security threats found in Proclamation 9704, 
   222                  Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 10962.
   223  
   224  [[Page 34087]]
   225  
   226                  11. Section 232 authorizes the President to adjust the 
   227                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   228                  being imported into the United States in such 
   229                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   230                  to impair the national security of the United States so 
   231                  that such imports will not threaten to impair the 
   232                  national security.
   233  
   234                  12. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended, 
   235                  19 U.S.C. 2483 (section 604), authorizes the President 
   236                  to embody in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the 
   237                  United States (HTSUS) the substance of statutes 
   238                  affecting import treatment, and actions thereunder, 
   239                  including the removal, modification, continuance, or 
   240                  imposition of any rate of duty or other import 
   241                  restriction.
   242  
   243                  NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the 
   244                  United States of America, by the authority vested in me 
   245                  by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, 
   246                  including section 232, section 604, and section 301 of 
   247                  title 3, United States Code, do hereby proclaim as 
   248                  follows:
   249  
   250                  (1) Effective with respect to goods entered for 
   251                  consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for 
   252                  consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight 
   253                  time on June 8, 2026, subchapter III of chapter 99 of 
   254                  the HTSUS is modified as provided in Annex IV to this 
   255                  proclamation and the lists of products provided in 
   256                  Annex I-A, Annex I-B, Annex II, and Annex III of 
   257                  Proclamation 11021 are modified as set forth in the 
   258                  annexes to this proclamation.
   259  
   260                  (2) Effective with respect to goods entered for 
   261                  consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for 
   262                  consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight 
   263                  time on June 8, 2026, until 11:59 p.m. eastern standard 
   264                  time on December 31, 2027, the applicable additional ad 
   265                  valorem rate of duty imposed pursuant to section 232 
   266                  under Proclamation 9704, as amended, and Proclamation 
   267                  9705, as amended, for all aluminum and steel articles 
   268                  listed in Annex I-C to this proclamation shall be:
   269  
   270                      (a) 25 percent, unless a lower rate of duty applies 
   271                  pursuant to clause (2)(b), (2)(c), or (2)(d) of this 
   272                  proclamation;
   273                      (b) For products of Argentina, Ecuador, El 
   274                  Salvador, Guatemala, Japan, the Republic of Korea, 
   275                  Liechtenstein, Switzerland, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, 
   276                  or a member nation of the European Union, the rate of 
   277                  duty shall be determined by the product's current ad 
   278                  valorem (or ad valorem equivalent) rate of duty under 
   279                  Column 1 of the HTSUS (Column 1 Duty Rate). For 
   280                  products of these jurisdictions with a Column 1 Duty 
   281                  Rate that is less than 15 percent, the sum of the 
   282                  Column 1 Duty Rate and the additional section 232 ad 
   283                  valorem rate of duty pursuant to this clause, shall be 
   284                  15 percent. For products of these jurisdictions with a 
   285                  Column 1 Duty Rate that is at least 15 percent, the 
   286                  additional section 232 ad valorem rate of duty imposed 
   287                  pursuant to this clause shall be zero percent;
   288                      (c) 10 percent, determined based on the product's 
   289                  current ad valorem (or ad valorem equivalent) Column 1 
   290                  Duty Rate in the same manner outlined in clause (2)(b) 
   291                  of this proclamation, for derivative articles the 
   292                  aluminum content of which is composed entirely of 
   293                  aluminum that was smelted and cast in the United 
   294                  States, or the steel content of which is composed 
   295                  entirely of steel that was melted and poured in the 
   296                  United States; and
   297                      (d) For products of Canada and Mexico that qualify 
   298                  for preferential tariff treatment under the United 
   299                  States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a duty of 25 percent 
   300                  shall apply only to the non-U.S. content of the 
   301                  product. For purposes of this clause, ``non-U.S. 
   302                  content'' means the total value of the product minus 
   303                  the value attributable to parts produced in the United 
   304                  States. Notwithstanding the foregoing, the total 
   305                  effective duty on the imported product assessed under 
   306                  this subclause shall not be less than 15 percent ad 
   307                  valorem, as detailed in Annex IV of this proclamation. 
   308                  The Secretary shall issue guidance to U.S. Customs and 
   309                  Border Protection (CBP) regarding the assessment of 
   310                  ``U.S. content'' for purposes of this clause. If CBP 
   311                  determines that an importer has engaged in fraud or has 
   312                  deliberately misled the United States Government 
   313                  regarding the United States content of an imported 
   314                  product, CBP shall impose penalties to the extent 
   315                  permitted by law.
   316  
   317  [[Page 34088]]
   318  
   319                  (3)(a) Effective with respect to goods entered for 
   320                  consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption 
   321                  on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time on January 
   322                  1, 2028, the applicable additional ad valorem rate of 
   323                  duty imposed under Proclamation 9704, as amended; 
   324                  Proclamation 9705, as amended; and Proclamation 10962, 
   325                  as amended, for imports of products listed in Annex I-C 
   326                  to this proclamation shall be the rates set out in 
   327                  clause (3) of Proclamation 11021.
   328  
   329                      (b) If a product is subject to multiple rates of 
   330                  duty under clause (2) of this proclamation, the lowest 
   331                  applicable rate of duty shall apply.
   332  
   333                  (4) For purposes of this proclamation and Proclamation 
   334                  11021, as set forth in Annex IV to this proclamation, a 
   335                  product's metal content shall be deemed composed 
   336                  entirely of aluminum that was smelted and cast in the

   343                  (5) The Secretary, in consultation with the United

   345                  Chair of the International Trade Commission, the 
   346                  Secretary of Homeland Security, and any other senior 
   347                  official the Secretary deems appropriate, shall 
   348                  determine whether any modifications to the HTSUS are 
   349                  necessary to effectuate or implement this proclamation 
   350                  or any actions taken pursuant to this proclamation, and

   353                  technical corrections to any annexes to this 
   354                  proclamation.

   356                  (6) The Secretary shall continue to monitor imports of 
   357                  metal products. The Secretary and the Trade

   360                  The Secretary and the Trade Representative shall inform 
   361                  the President of any circumstances that, in their 
   362                  opinion, might indicate the need for further

    93                  By the President of the United States of America

    95                  A Proclamation
    96  
    97                  1. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    98                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), as 
    99                  amended, I found, under section 232 of the Trade 
   100                  Expansion Act of 1962, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1862 
   101                  (section 232), that aluminum is being imported into the 
   102                  United States in such quantities or under such 
   103                  circumstances as to threaten to impair the national 
   104                  security of the United States. To address the national 
   105                  security threat found in Proclamation 9704, I 
   106                  established a tariff regime, which included imposing ad 
   107                  valorem duties on certain imports of aluminum articles 
   108                  and its derivative articles. In subsequent 
   109                  proclamations, including Proclamation 11021 of April 2, 
   110                  2026 (Strengthening Actions Taken To Adjust Imports of 
   111                  Aluminum, Steel, and Copper Into the United States), 
   112                  and Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026 (Further 
   113                  Adjusting the Tariff Regimes for Imports of Aluminum,

   115                  the tariff regime for aluminum to more effectively 
   116                  address the national security threat found in 
   117                  Proclamation 9704.
   118  
   119                  2. In those proclamations, I directed the Secretary of 
   120                  Commerce (Secretary) to monitor the effects of imports 
   121                  of aluminum with respect to the national security, to 
   122                  update me on the status of that threat to the national 
   123                  security, and to provide me with recommendations if

   125                  Presidential action under section 232.
   126  
   127                  3. Based on the Secretary's monitoring, I have received

   129                  Secretary regarding the tariff regime imposed in

   133                  4. Among other things, the Secretary has informed me 
   134                  that the additional ad valorem duties on imports of 
   135                  aluminum are strengthening the American aluminum 
   136                  industries and addressing the national security threat 
   137                  found in Proclamation 9704. In the Secretary's opinion, 
   138                  domestic aluminum production and related domestic 
   139                  aluminum industry would not be as strong as they are if 
   140                  not for the aluminum tariff regime imposed under 
   141                  section 232, and the national security threat found in 
   142                  Proclamation 9704 would be worse than it is if not for 
   143                  the aluminum tariff regime imposed under section 232.
   144  
   145                  5. The Secretary has informed and advised me of his 
   146                  opinion that, despite the benefits from the aluminum 
   147                  tariff regime, the domestic production and supply of 
   148                  primary aluminum, which is critical to the U.S. economy 
   149                  and defense industrial base, is still in insufficient 
   150                  supply. In the Secretary's view, it is important to 
   151                  modify the aluminum tariff regime in a way to more 
   152                  effectively encourage increased domestic production of 
   153                  primary aluminum.
   154  
   155                  6. To ensure that the aluminum tariff regime continues

   158                  that I establish an incentive for companies to engage 
   159                  in building new facilities capable of producing primary 
   160                  aluminum, expanding facilities
   161  
   162  [[Page 46636]]
   163  
   164                  to become capable of producing primary aluminum, or 
   165                  refurbishing outdated facilities that produce primary 
   166                  aluminum to expand their production or increase the 
   167                  efficiency of production. The Secretary recommended 
   168                  that I do this by allowing those companies or their 
   169                  designated representatives to import a quantity of 
   170                  primary aluminum corresponding to the reasonably 
   171                  anticipated annual production of primary aluminum from 
   172                  the new project at a reduced tariff rate. This would 
   173                  build on the program established for certain aluminum 
   174                  and steel from Canada and Mexico in clause 13 of 
   175                  Proclamation 10984 of October 17, 2025 (Adjusting 
   176                  Imports of Medium- and Heavy-Duty Vehicles, Medium- and 
   177                  Heavy-Duty Vehicle Parts, and Buses Into the United 
   178                  States).
   179  
   180                  7. After considering the current information, opinions, 
   181                  and recommendations newly provided by the Secretary; 
   182                  the factors in section 232 (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)); the 
   183                  need to address the national security threat found in 
   184                  Proclamation 9704; and other relevant factors and 
   185                  information, I have determined that it is necessary and 
   186                  appropriate to modify the tariff regime for imports of 
   187                  aluminum imposed in Proclamation 9704, as amended. In 
   188                  particular, I determine that it is necessary and 
   189                  appropriate to establish an investment incentive 
   190                  program for companies investing in new U.S. production 
   191                  capacity for primary aluminum, as further detailed 
   192                  below. In my judgment, the modifications in this 
   193                  proclamation will ensure that the tariff regime imposed 
   194                  on imports of aluminum continue to effectively address 
   195                  the national security threat found in Proclamation 
   196                  9704.
   197

   199                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   200                  being imported into the United States in such 
   201                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   202                  to impair the national security of the United States so 
   203                  that such imports will not threaten to impair the 
   204                  national security.
   205  
   206                  9. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
   207                  U.S.C. 2483) (section 604), authorizes the President to 
   208                  embody in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United 
   209                  States (HTSUS) the substance of statutes affecting 
   210                  import treatment, and actions thereunder, including the 
   211                  removal, modification, continuance, or imposition of 
   212                  any rate of duty or other import restriction.
   213  
   214                  NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the 
   215                  United States of America, by the authority vested in me 
   216                  by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, 
   217                  including section 232, section 604, and section 301 of 
   218                  title 3, United States Code, do hereby proclaim as 
   219                  follows:

   221  (1) The Secretary is authorized to and shall establish a program to

   231  
   232    (b) The Secretary is authorized to approve onshoring plans described in

   241  anticipated costs and primary-aluminum production projections are 
   242  reasonable, and how the benefits of the reduced tariff rate will be 
   243  allocated between the applicants of the onshoring plan. When approving 
   244  onshoring plans, the Secretary shall act in a manner consistent with the 
   245  need to address the national security threat found in Proclamation 9704.
   246

   248  
   249    (c) If the Secretary approves a company's onshoring plan, the Secretary
