   140                  section 122, the purposes of section 122, and the 
   141                  national interest of the United States.
   142  
   143  [[Page 9340]]
   144  
   145                  6. Among other things, I have been informed by my 
   146                  advisors that the United States balance-of-payments 
   147                  position, under any reasonable understanding of the 
   148                  term in the context of section 122, is currently a 
   149                  large and serious deficit. My advisors have studied 
   150                  different methods of evaluating balance-of-payments 
   151                  deficits, including calculations based on current-
   152                  account statistics. In my advisors' opinions, under any 
   153                  of these methods, the United States balance-of-payments 
   154                  position is a large and serious deficit.
   155  
   156                  7. For instance, my advisors have informed me that the 
   157                  United States runs a deficit in selling goods and 
   158                  services overseas, as reported by the United States 
   159                  Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) in the ``balance on 
   160                  goods and services''; has recently reflected quarterly 
   161                  deficits in its return on investment or labor, as 
   162                  reported by the BEA in the ``balance on primary 
   163                  income''; and runs a deficit in voluntary transfers, 
   164                  such as remittances, as reported by the BEA in the 
   165                  ``balance on secondary income.'' In other words, the 
   166                  United States runs a trade deficit, does not currently 
   167                  make a net income from the capital and labor that it 
   168                  deploys abroad, and experiences more transfer payments, 
   169                  on net, flowing out of the country than into the 
   170                  country.
   171  
   172                  8. As my advisors have informed me, the United States 
   173                  runs a substantial trade deficit. The large, 
   174                  persistent, and serious annual United States goods 
   175                  trade deficit has grown by over 40 percent in the past 
   176                  5 years alone, reaching $1.2 trillion in 2024. In 2025, 
   177                  the United States goods trade deficit remained at 
   178                  approximately $1.2 trillion. The effects of this 
   179                  deficit are serious, and this deficit contributes to 
   180                  the fundamental international payments problems facing 
   181                  the United States.
   182  
   183                  9. As my advisors have also informed me, the annual 
   184                  balance on the United States primary income turned 
   185                  negative for the first time since at least 1960 in 
   186                  2024. From 1960 to 2023, the United States ran a 
   187                  surplus in its annual balance on primary income. That 
   188                  positive balance on primary income served as a 
   189                  stabilizing force for the United States balance-of-
   190                  payments position even in the face of large and 
   191                  persistent trade deficits. In 2024, however, the 
   192                  balance on primary income turned negative and thus 
   193                  ceased to serve as a counterweight to the trade deficit 
   194                  in the United States current account. Indeed, in 2024, 
   195                  the United States maintained a current account deficit 
   196                  of 4.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), almost 
   197                  double the current account deficit of approximately 2.0 
   198                  percent that prevailed between 2013 and 2019, and 
   199                  larger than that which prevailed from 2019 to 2023. As 
   200                  a share of GDP, the staggering deficit of 4.0 percent 
   201                  represented the biggest annual current account deficit 
   202                  since 2008.
   203  
   204                  10. As my advisors have also informed me, the net 
   205                  international-investment position of the United States 
   206                  is in an ongoing decline. According to the BEA, at the 
   207                  end of 2024, the net international-investment position 
   208                  of the United States, as a share of GDP, was negative 
   209                  90 percent, a sharp deterioration from the average of 
   210                  negative 41 percent in the decade between 2010 and 
   211                  2020. In my advisors' view, this is a highly atypical 
   212                  position for a country, particularly the United States. 
   213                  Indeed, both in terms of United States dollars and as a 
   214                  share of GDP, this represents one of the most negative 
   215                  net international-investment positions of any developed 
   216                  country. Because the current account is one of the 
   217                  primary drivers of changes in the net international-
   218                  investment position, the atypically large negative net 
   219                  international-investment position of the United States 
   220                  shows that the United States balance-of-payments 
   221                  deficit is large and serious.
   222  
   223                  11. Further, as my advisors have informed me, the 
   224                  balance on secondary income of the United States has 
   225                  been persistently in a deficit since the 1960s.
   226  
   227                  12. According to my advisors, an import surcharge in 
   228                  the form of ad valorem duties is required to address 
   229                  these fundamental international payments problems. In 
   230                  my advisors' opinions, imposing an import surcharge 
   231                  would deal with the large and serious United States 
   232                  balance-of-payments deficit. My advisors have further 
   233                  recommended that certain products should not be subject 
   234                  to the surcharge because of the needs of the United 
   235                  States economy
   236  
   237  [[Page 9341]]
   238  
   239                  and have opined that a surcharge with certain 
   240                  exceptions would more effectively deal with the 
   241                  balance-of-payments deficit than would a surcharge 
   242                  without the exceptions.
   243  
   244                  13. After considering the information, opinions, and 
   245                  recommendations that have been provided to me by senior 
   246                  officials, among other relevant information and 
   247                  considerations, I find that fundamental international 
   248                  payments problems within the meaning of section 122 
   249                  exist; that those problems significantly harm United 
   250                  States national interests, including economic and 
   251                  national security interests; and that special measures 
   252                  to restrict imports are required to address those 
   253                  problems, as authorized by section 122. Specifically, I 
   254                  find that a surcharge in the form of ad valorem duties 
   255                  on certain imports is required to deal with the United 
   256                  States' large and serious balance-of-payments deficit. 
   257                  Accordingly, I impose, for a period of 150 days, a 
   258                  temporary import surcharge of 10 percent ad valorem, as 
   259                  described below, on articles imported into the United 
   260                  States, effective February 24, 2026.
   261  
   262                  14. Because of the needs of the United States economy, 
   263                  I determine that the surcharge imposed in this 
   264                  proclamation shall not apply to the following products, 
   265                  as further detailed in Annexes I and II to this 
   266                  proclamation:

   268                  (a) certain critical minerals;
   269  
   270                  (b) metals used in currency and bullion;
   271  
   272                  (c) energy and energy products;
   273  
   274                  (d) natural resources and fertilizers that cannot be 
   275                  grown, mined, or otherwise produced in the United 
   276                  States or grown, mined, or otherwise produced in 
   277                  sufficient quantities to meet domestic demand;
   278  
   279                  (e) certain agricultural products, including beef, 
   280                  tomatoes, and oranges;
   281

   283

   286                  (h) passenger vehicles, certain light trucks, certain 
   287                  medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, buses, and certain 
   288                  parts of passenger vehicles, light trucks, medium- and

    38                  Section 1. Purpose. The United States has imposed 
    39                  tariffs under various statutory authorities and through 
    40                  a number of Executive Orders and proclamations to

    42                  extraordinary threats to the national security, foreign 
    43                  policy, and economy of the United States. Although each 
    44                  of these actions, as listed in section 2 of this order,

    48                  a cumulative effect (or ``stack'' on top of one 
    49                  another) because the rate of duty resulting from such 
    50                  stacking exceeds what is necessary to achieve the 
    51                  intended policy goals. To avoid the cumulative effect 
    52                  of overlapping tariffs on certain articles, this order 
    53                  sets out the procedure for determining which of 
    54                  multiple tariffs shall apply to an article when that 
    55                  article is subject to more than one of the actions 
    56                  listed in section 2 of this order.

   104                  Sec. 3. Non-Stacking of Tariff Measures. (a) 
   105                  Notwithstanding any provision of any action listed in 
   106                  section 2 of this order, tariffs for articles subject 
   107                  to tariffs under the actions listed in section 2 of

    34                  By the President of the United States of America
    35  
    36                  A Proclamation
    37  
    38                  1. On January 11, 2018, the Secretary of Commerce 
    39                  (Secretary) transmitted to me a report on the 
    40                  Secretary's investigation into the effect of imports of 
    41                  steel mill articles (steel articles) on the national 
    42                  security of the United States under section 232 of the 
    43                  Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended (19 U.S.C. 
    44                  1862) (section 232). The Secretary found and advised me 
    45                  of his opinion that steel articles are being imported 
    46                  into the United States in such quantities and under 
    47                  such circumstances as to threaten to impair the 
    48                  national security of the United States.
    49  
    50                  2. In Proclamation 9705 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    51                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), and 
    52                  Proclamation 9980 of January 24, 2020 (Adjusting 
    53                  Imports of Derivative Aluminum Articles and Derivative 
    54                  Steel Articles Into the United States), I concurred 
    55                  with the Secretary's findings that steel articles, as 
    56                  defined in clause 1 of Proclamation 9705, and 
    57                  derivative steel articles, as described in clause 3 of 
    58                  Proclamation 9980, are being imported into the United 
    59                  States in such quantities and under such circumstances 
    60                  as to threaten to impair the national security of the 
    61                  United States, and I decided to adjust the imports of 
    62                  those steel articles and derivative steel articles by 
    63                  imposing a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    64                  articles imported from most countries. In Proclamation 
    65                  10896 of February 10, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Steel 
    66                  Into the United States), I decided to adjust the 
    67                  imports of steel articles and derivative steel articles 
    68                  by imposing a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    69                  articles imported from all countries.
    70  
    71                  3. On January 19, 2018, the Secretary transmitted to me 
    72                  a report on the Secretary's investigation into the 
    73                  effect of imports of aluminum articles on the national 
    74                  security of the United States under section 232. The 
    75                  Secretary found and advised me of his opinion that 
    76                  aluminum articles are being imported into the United 
    77                  States in such quantities and under such circumstances 
    78                  as to threaten to impair the national security of the 
    79                  United States.
    80  
    81                  4. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    82                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), and 
    83                  Proclamation 9980, I concurred with the Secretary's 
    84                  findings that aluminum articles, as defined in clause 1 
    85                  of Proclamation 9704, and derivative aluminum articles, 
    86                  as described in clause 3 of Proclamation 9980, are 
    87                  being imported into the United States in such 
    88                  quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten 
    89                  to impair the national security of the United States, 
    90                  and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum articles 
    91                  and derivative aluminum articles by imposing a 10 
    92                  percent ad valorem tariff on such articles imported 
    93                  from most countries. In Proclamation 10895 of February 
    94                  10, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Aluminum Into the United 
    95                  States), I decided to adjust the imports of aluminum 
    96                  articles and derivative aluminum articles by imposing a 
    97                  25 percent ad valorem tariff on such articles imported 
    98                  from all countries.
    99  
   100                  5. In Proclamation 10896 and Proclamation 10895, I 
   101                  instructed the Secretary to continue to monitor imports 
   102                  of steel articles and derivative steel articles, and 
   103                  aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles, 
   104                  respectively, and
   105  
   106  [[Page 24200]]
   107  
   108                  to review the status of such imports with respect to 
   109                  the national security of the United States. The 
   110                  Secretary has done so and has advised me accordingly.
   111  
   112                  6. After considering current information newly provided 
   113                  by the Secretary, among other things, I have determined 
   114                  that it is necessary to increase the previously 
   115                  described steel and aluminum tariffs to adjust the 
   116                  imports of steel and aluminum articles and their 
   117                  derivative articles so that such imports will not 
   118                  threaten to impair the national security. In my 
   119                  judgment, the increased tariffs will more effectively 
   120                  counter foreign countries that continue to offload low-
   121                  priced, excess steel and aluminum in the United States 
   122                  market and thereby undercut the competitiveness of the 
   123                  United States steel and aluminum industries. Although 
   124                  the previously imposed steel and aluminum tariffs have 
   125                  helped provide critical price support in the United 
   126                  States market, they have not yet enabled these 
   127                  industries to develop and maintain the rates of 
   128                  capacity production utilization that are necessary for 
   129                  the industries' sustained health and for projected 
   130                  national defense needs. I have determined that 
   131                  increasing the previously imposed tariffs will provide 
   132                  greater support to these industries and reduce or 
   133                  eliminate the national security threat posed by imports 
   134                  of steel and aluminum articles and their derivative 
   135                  articles.

   162                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   163                  being imported into the United States in such 
   164                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   165                  to impair the national security.

   173                  duty or other import restriction.

   199  
   200                  daylight time on June 4, 2025, and shall continue in

   203                      (3) Any imports of articles set forth in Annex II

   205                  States foreign trade zone under ``privileged foreign 
   206                  status'' as defined in 19 CFR 146.41 before 12:01 a.m.

   261                  Kingdom that would otherwise be applicable pursuant to

   263                  amended; Proclamation 9980, as amended; Proclamation 
   264                  10895; and Proclamation 10896 shall remain at 25

    25  Guidance to U.S. Customs and Border Protection Regarding the 
    26  Assessment of ``U.S. Content'' for Purposes of Implementing Tariffs 
    27  Pursuant to Clause (2)(D) of Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026
    28  
    29  AGENCY: Bureau of Industry and Security, Department of Commerce.
    30  
    31  ACTION: Notice.
    32  
    33  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    34  
    35  SUMMARY: This notice provides guidance to U.S. Customs and Border 
    36  Protection regarding the assessment of ``U.S. content'' for products of 
    37  Canada and Mexico that qualify for preferential tariff treatment under 
    38  the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, for purposes of implementing 
    39  tariffs pursuant to Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026.
    40  
    41  DATES: The guidance set out in in this notice is effective with respect 
    42  to products that are entered for consumption, or withdrawn from 
    43  warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern Time on 
    44  October 14, 2026.
    45  
    46  SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
    47  
    48  Background
    49  
    50      On June 1, 2026, the President issued Presidential Proclamation 
    51  11032 entitled ``Further Adjusting the Tariff Regimes for Imports of 
    52  Aluminum, Steel, and Copper into the United States'' (91 FR 34085) 
    53  (Proclamation). The Proclamation modifies the tariff regimes for metal 
    54  products imposed in Presidential Proclamation 9704, as amended, 
    55  Proclamation 9705, as amended, and Proclamation 10962, as amended, and 
    56  directs the Secretary of Commerce (Secretary) to issue guidance to U.S. 
    57  Customs and Border Protection regarding the assessment of ``U.S. 
    58  content'' for purposes of implementing tariffs pursuant to clause 
    59  (2)(d) of the Proclamation. The Secretary has delegated this duty to 
    60  the Deputy Assistant Secretary for Technology Security.
    61  
    62  Guidance to U.S. Customs and Border Protection Regarding the Assessment 
    63  of ``U.S. Content'' for Purposes of Implementing Tariffs Pursuant to 
    64  Clause (2)(d) of Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026
    65  
    66      The Department of Commerce advises that, for purposes of 
    67  implementing clause (2)(d) of the Proclamation, the term ``U.S. 
    68  content'' means the following:
    69      1. The value of the product attributable to parts wholly obtained, 
    70  entirely produced, or substantially transformed in the United States, 
    71  and
    72      2. To the extent not otherwise accounted for in (1), the value of 
    73  the product attributable to steel that was melted and poured in the 
    74  United States, aluminum that was smelted and cast in the United States, 
    75  and/or copper that was smelted and cast in the United States.
    76      Questions regarding the application of this Notice to a specific 
    77  product may be directed to U.S. Customs and Border Protection.
    78  
    79  Jessica Curyto,
    80  Deputy Assistant Secretary for Technology Security.

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

  "Q1": {
    "answer": "(a) The section 338 presidential series published through November 14, 2026 consists of these ten proclamations. Times below are Eastern.

| Proclamation | FR document; first-page citation | Signed | Published | Operative change and applicable event |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 11046 | 2026-14991; 91 FR 46639 | July 20, 2026 | July 23, 2026 | Imposes 50% duties on its Annex II Canadian products in response to alcoholic-beverage discrimination. As printed, applies to consumption entries and warehouse withdrawals for consumption from August 19, 2026, 12:01 a.m.; subsequently delayed to August 22 by 11056. |
| 11047 | 2026-14992; 91 FR 46653 | July 20, 2026 | July 23, 2026 | Same initial duty and entry/withdrawal dates for its Annex II products, addressing dairy discrimination; subsequently delayed by 11056. |
| 11048 | 2026-14997; 91 FR 46663 | July 20, 2026 | July 23, 2026 | Same initial duty and entry/withdrawal dates for its Annex II products, addressing motor-vehicle discrimination; subsequently delayed by 11056. |
| 11056 | 2026-17294; 91 FR 54789 | August 18, 2026 | August 24, 2026 | Delays all three duties to August 22, 2026, 12:01 a.m. The relevant events remain consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal for consumption under the original proclamations. |
| 11061 | 2026-18835; 91 FR 58311 | September 8, 2026 | September 14, 2026 | Excludes its Annex Canadian alcoholic beverages from importation beginning September 29, 2026, 12:01 a.m. The trigger is importation, not consumption entry. Preserves the 50% duty for covered goods imported before the ban but not yet consumption-entered or withdrawn. |
| 11062 | 2026-18836; 91 FR 58319 | September 8, 2026 | September 14, 2026 | Corresponding dairy import exclusion and pre-ban-import savings rule; importation trigger September 29, 2026, 12:01 a.m. |
| 11063 | 2026-18837; 91 FR 58325 | September 8, 2026 | September 14, 2026 | Corresponding motor-vehicle-series import exclusion and savings rule; importation trigger September 29, 2026, 12:01 a.m. |
| 11064 | 2026-18838; 91 FR 58331 | September 8, 2026 | September 14, 2026 | Adds Annex I, Part A products to the alcoholic-beverage-series duty, removes Part B products, and makes the modified duty cumulative with section 232. Applies to consumption entries and warehouse withdrawals from September 15, 2026, 12:01 a.m. |
| 11065 | 2026-18839; 91 FR 58339 | September 8, 2026 | September 14, 2026 | Makes the corresponding Part A additions, Part B removals, and section 232 stacking change for the motor-vehicle series, using the same September 15 entry/withdrawal trigger. |
| 11076 | 2026-22292; 91 FR 68861 | October 23, 2026 | October 30, 2026 | Further changes motor-vehicle-series scope, this time removing Annex I, Part A products and adding Part B products. Applies to consumption entries and warehouse withdrawals from October 30, 2026, 12:01 a.m.; retains section 232 stacking. |

(b) Product-scope changes:
- **Alcoholic-beverage series:** 11046 establishes the initial Annex II scope; 11064 adds its Part A and removes its Part B and removes the readable section 232 shield; 11061 changes its Annex products from tariff treatment to an import ban, subject to its savings and invalidation provisions.
- **Dairy series:** 11047 establishes the initial Annex II scope; 11062 changes its Annex products to an import ban, subject to its savings and invalidation provisions. No actual dairy scope-modification proclamation was found. Its reference to one does not supply an operative scope amendment.
- **Motor-vehicle series:** 11048 establishes the initial Annex II scope; 11065 adds its Part A, removes its Part B, and removes the section 232 shield; 11063 changes its Annex products to an import ban; 11076 subsequently removes its Part A and adds its Part B.
- 11056 changes timing, not product coverage.",

  "Q2": {
    "answer": "(a) Section 338 duty:
- Entry 1, August 20 at 2:00 p.m.: $40,000 × 0% = **$0**.
- Entry 2, August 21 at 11:59 p.m.: $40,000 × 0% = **$0**.
- Entry 3, August 22 at 12:01 a.m.: $40,000 × 50% = **$20,000**.
The controlling replacement start is August 22 at 12:01 a.m., inclusive, under Proclamation 11056, clause (1), FR Doc. 2026-17294, 91 FR 54790.

(b) Clause (1) of 11056 first declares that the effective date of the duties in all three original proclamations “shall be” August 22 at 12:01 a.m. It then expressly amends the **chapeau of Annex II** of each original proclamation, replacing “August 19, 2026” with “August 22, 2026.” It does not expressly rewrite the August 19 language printed in clauses (1) and (3) of 11046 or its recital 9. The new substantive effective-date command, together with 11056's clause (5) superseding inconsistent earlier provisions, resolves the difference in favor of August 22.

(c) The excess deposit was $40,000 × 50% = **$20,000**. Clause (4) of 11056 says that, to the extent implementation requires refunds, they “shall be processed pursuant to applicable law and CBP's standard procedures.” It does not identify a particular filing, deadline, or automatic-payment mechanism.

(d) **No further presidential activation was required.** Clause (1) of 11056 sets an unconditional replacement date. Later recitals state that Canada expressed a commitment to remove the discrimination, reneged and ceased good-faith negotiations on August 21, and that the suspension lapsed and duties became effective at 12:01 a.m. on August 22. Those later recitals report what happened; they are not a new activation clause.

(e) The original proclamation describes a minimum 30-day waiting period after the President's discrimination-finding proclamation. It was signed July 20:
- July 20 to July 31 = 11 days.
- July 31 to August 19 = 19 days.
- 11 + 19 = **30 days**.
Thus the original August 19 date corresponds to 30 calendar days after signing, not 30 days after the July 23 publication.",
    "basis": "Proclamation 11046, recital 9 and recital 10, FR Doc. 2026-14991, 91 FR 46640, and clauses (1) and (3), 91 FR 46641. Proclamation 11056, clauses (1)–(2), FR Doc. 2026-17294, 91 FR 54790; refund clause (4) and supersession clause (5), 91 FR 54791. Negotiation explanation: 11056, recitals 4–5, 91 FR 54790. Subsequent account of August 21 and automatic lapse: Proclamation 11061, recitals 2–4, FR Doc. 2026-18835, 91 FR 58311; also Proclamation 11064, recitals 2–4, FR Doc. 2026-18838, 91 FR 58331.",
    "uncertainty": "The documents do not specify the procedural vehicle or deadline for recovering this particular deposit. The calendar arithmetic establishes the intended original 30-day interval; no signing time is supplied."

  "Q3": {
    "answer": "(a) The ban turns on **importation**, whereas the tariff ordinarily turns on consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal.
- **A:** May be imported. It arrives and is entered before the ban. Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
- **B:** May be imported. Its September 27 importation is grandfathered even though warehouse withdrawal occurs October 5. Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
- **C:** May be imported. Its September 28, 11:30 p.m. importation precedes the September 29, 12:01 a.m. cutoff; the following morning's entry does not defeat the savings clause. Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
- **D:** Importation is prohibited. Arrival at 12:30 a.m. on September 29 is after the cutoff. There is **no lawful consumption entry under these facts**; paying 50% is not an alternative to the prohibition. No ordinary section 338 duty total can be assigned to a permitted entry.

(b) **E:** The most defensible reading is that the September 25 importation is grandfathered by clause (2) of 11061. It remains subject to the tariff on October 6, not to the ban:
- Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
The original duty proclamation also requires privileged foreign status for covered zone admissions after its effective date, unless domestic status is available. The exclusion proclamation does not expressly discuss zones, but its savings language covers products “imported, but not yet entered for consumption.”

(c) Clause (9)(b) supplies a **50% tariff fallback** if the ban is invalidated as to an import. The defensible prospective treatment for this beer after an applicable invalidation is the restored/original 50% duty, rather than duty-free access:
- Section 338 on a $30,000 shipment: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
The precise effect of a particular judgment would depend on its scope; the proclamation's wording does not itself resolve every temporal question about invalidation.

(d) **No.** Clause (3) says the exclusion proclamation does not otherwise affect the tariff-covered products, apart from changing its Annex products to import-ban treatment. Products outside the exclusion Annex retain their applicable tariff treatment under 11046 as modified by 11064.",

Q2.answer:
(a) Section 338 duty:
- Entry 1, August 20 at 2:00 p.m.: $40,000 × 0% = **$0**.
- Entry 2, August 21 at 11:59 p.m.: $40,000 × 0% = **$0**.
- Entry 3, August 22 at 12:01 a.m.: $40,000 × 50% = **$20,000**.
The controlling replacement start is August 22 at 12:01 a.m., inclusive, under Proclamation 11056, clause (1), FR Doc. 2026-17294, 91 FR 54790.

(b) Clause (1) of 11056 first declares that the effective date of the duties in all three original proclamations “shall be” August 22 at 12:01 a.m. It then expressly amends the **chapeau of Annex II** of each original proclamation, replacing “August 19, 2026” with “August 22, 2026.” It does not expressly rewrite the August 19 language printed in clauses (1) and (3) of 11046 or its recital 9. The new substantive effective-date command, together with 11056's clause (5) superseding inconsistent earlier provisions, resolves the difference in favor of August 22.

(c) The excess deposit was $40,000 × 50% = **$20,000**. Clause (4) of 11056 says that, to the extent implementation requires refunds, they “shall be processed pursuant to applicable law and CBP's standard procedures.” It does not identify a particular filing, deadline, or automatic-payment mechanism.

(d) **No further presidential activation was required.** Clause (1) of 11056 sets an unconditional replacement date. Later recitals state that Canada expressed a commitment to remove the discrimination, reneged and ceased good-faith negotiations on August 21, and that the suspension lapsed and duties became effective at 12:01 a.m. on August 22. Those later recitals report what happened; they are not a new activation clause.

(e) The original proclamation describes a minimum 30-day waiting period after the President's discrimination-finding proclamation. It was signed July 20:
- July 20 to July 31 = 11 days.
- July 31 to August 19 = 19 days.
- 11 + 19 = **30 days**.
Thus the original August 19 date corresponds to 30 calendar days after signing, not 30 days after the July 23 publication.

Q3.answer:
(a) The ban turns on **importation**, whereas the tariff ordinarily turns on consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal.
- **A:** May be imported. It arrives and is entered before the ban. Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
- **B:** May be imported. Its September 27 importation is grandfathered even though warehouse withdrawal occurs October 5. Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
- **C:** May be imported. Its September 28, 11:30 p.m. importation precedes the September 29, 12:01 a.m. cutoff; the following morning's entry does not defeat the savings clause. Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
- **D:** Importation is prohibited. Arrival at 12:30 a.m. on September 29 is after the cutoff. There is **no lawful consumption entry under these facts**; paying 50% is not an alternative to the prohibition. No ordinary section 338 duty total can be assigned to a permitted entry.

(b) **E:** The most defensible reading is that the September 25 importation is grandfathered by clause (2) of 11061. It remains subject to the tariff on October 6, not to the ban:
- Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
The original duty proclamation also requires privileged foreign status for covered zone admissions after its effective date, unless domestic status is available. The exclusion proclamation does not expressly discuss zones, but its savings language covers products “imported, but not yet entered for consumption.”

(c) Clause (9)(b) supplies a **50% tariff fallback** if the ban is invalidated as to an import. The defensible prospective treatment for this beer after an applicable invalidation is the restored/original 50% duty, rather than duty-free access:
- Section 338 on a $30,000 shipment: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
The precise effect of a particular judgment would depend on its scope; the proclamation's wording does not itself resolve every temporal question about invalidation.

(d) **No.** Clause (3) says the exclusion proclamation does not otherwise affect the tariff-covered products, apart from changing its Annex products to import-ban treatment. Products outside the exclusion Annex retain their applicable tariff treatment under 11046 as modified by 11064.
Q3.basis: Proclamation 11061, clause (1) (importation cutoff), clause (2) (pre-ban imports retain 50%), clause (3) (other tariff scope unchanged), and clause (9)(b) (invalidation fallback), FR Doc. 2026-18835, 91 FR 58312–13. Original tariff and zone rule: Proclamation 11046, clauses (1), (3), and (4), FR Doc. 2026-14991, 91 FR 46641; replacement effective date: Proclamation 11056, clause (1), FR Doc. 2026-17294, 91 FR 54790.
Q3.uncertainty: 11061 contains no express FTZ transition provision; E's result follows from the stipulated importation date and the broad savings language, read with 11046's zone rule. Q11.answer:
(a) **The memorandum describes June's textile proposal as zero-rated, although June left the reduced rate open.** The July memorandum says USTR proposed a mechanism allowing a volume of textile/apparel imports at a “zero section 301 tariff rate” (FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47719). June actually proposed a “reduced Section 301 tariff rate” and solicited comments on the tariff rate, “if any” (FR Doc. 2026-11296, section IV, 91 FR 34274, and section VI, 91 FR 34275). The July notice itself accurately calls the proposal reduced-rate (FR Doc. 2026-15181, section I, 91 FR 47318). The discrepancy is the historical description, not the later decision to adopt zero-rate TRQs.

(b) **The July notice's chemicals-only retention account is broader than the adopted section 232 exemption.** Section III.C says it exempted all products proposed for exemption in Annex A except non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemicals, and “determined not to remove additional products” (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47330). June's readable Annex A expressly excludes “all articles and parts of articles that are subject to section 232 tariffs” (FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34276). Adopted note 52(a) affirmatively imposes the duty on all covered products except specified exceptions; note 52(f) supplies an enumerated set of headings/categories, not that blanket section 232 rule (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47352, 47362–63). Thus the chemicals-only account does not describe the full narrowing of the readable exemption framework.

(c) **The same chemicals-only account does not preserve June's categorical informational-materials and donations language.** June's Annex A expressly says the proposal “does not cover informational materials, donations” (FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34276). Adoption instead establishes the all-products rule with the enumerated exceptions in note 52(a)–(k); it does not enact those two blanket categories (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47352–94). This is a mismatch with the affirmative retention account in III.C, 91 FR 47330—not a finding that every book or every donation is taxable, since itemized or chapter 98 exceptions may still cover an article.

(d) **Accompanied baggage is narrowed despite the chemicals-only account.** June's Annex A excludes “accompanied baggage” without the later qualifier (FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34276). Adopted note 52(a) excepts “products for personal use included in accompanied baggage of persons arriving in the United States” (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47352), whereas III.C's retention account says the only cutback is non-pharmaceutical chemical applications (91 FR 47330).

(e) **USMCA coverage is described differently in the proposal and the retained-exemptions account.** June's readable Annex A says “USMCA-compliant goods of Canada or Mexico” are outside the proposal (FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34276). Adopted notes 52(g)–(h) require products of Canada or Mexico to be “entered free of duty” under USMCA (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47363). That actual-entry condition is more specific than compliance alone and is another qualification not captured by III.C's chemicals-only retention statement (91 FR 47330).

(f) **MFN-only descriptions do not fully describe the adopted South Korea calculation.** The memorandum directs netting against MFN, and the notice's South Korea determination repeatedly describes the base as MFN (FR Doc. 2026-15274, section 1(a)(ii), 91 FR 47720; FR Doc. 2026-15181, II.B.49, 91 FR 47327). Adopted note 52(k), however, expressly says that for South Korean goods with a properly claimed specific or compound **column 1-Special** rate, the equivalent is calculated using that rate; its netting paragraphs refer to the applicable “column 1 duty rate” (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47394). The readable operative note therefore supplies a Special-rate qualification not reflected in the MFN-only account.

(g) **The dairy exclusion proclamation cross-refers to a dairy scope proclamation that the published series does not supply.** Clause (3) of 11062 says the tariff scope was “further established” in a September 8 proclamation titled Modifying the Scope ... With Respect to Dairy (FR Doc. 2026-18836, 91 FR 58320). The actual September 8 scope texts are 11064, whose clause (1) modifies **11046/alcohol**, and 11065, whose clause (1) modifies **11048/motor vehicles** (FR Docs. 2026-18838 and 2026-18839, 91 FR 58332, 58340). Neither modifies 11047. The affirmative dairy cross-reference cannot substitute for a dairy scope amendment.

(h) **There is a resolved facial start-date inconsistency in the Canada texts.** The original operative clauses (1) and (3) still print August 19 (FR Docs. 2026-14991, 2026-14992, 2026-14997, 91 FR 46641, 46654–55, 46665). 11056 expressly changes the Annex II chapeaux, not those clauses, while substantively commanding August 22 at 12:01 a.m. and superseding inconsistent earlier provisions (FR Doc. 2026-17294, clauses (1) and (5), 91 FR 54790–91). This is not two equally operative dates: the later command resolves it. Later recitals expressly report the August 22 lapse and commencement (e.g. FR Doc. 2026-18835, recital 4, 91 FR 58311).

- Recognized U.S. content: $20,000 + $30,000 = $50,000, without double counting.
- Non-U.S. content: $200,000 − $50,000 = $150,000.
- Content-based duty: $150,000 × 25% = $37,500.
- Minimum: $200,000 × 15% = $30,000.
- **Section 232 owed: $37,500**.

(f) Same facts, October 6 entry, before the later guidance takes effect:
- U.S.-produced-parts value recognized by the proclamation's own definition: $20,000.
- Non-U.S. content: $200,000 − $20,000 = $180,000.
- Content-based duty: $180,000 × 25% = $45,000.
- Minimum: $200,000 × 15% = $30,000.
- **Section 232 owed on the readable text then applicable: $45,000**. The October 14 guidance does not state that its added metal-value recognition applies retroactively.

(g) Canadian USMCA machine with $140,000 U.S.-produced parts:
- Non-U.S. content: $200,000 − $140,000 = $60,000.
- Content-based duty: $60,000 × 25% = $15,000.
- Minimum: $200,000 × 15% = $30,000.
- **Section 232 owed: $30,000**.

(h) The temporary Annex I-C treatment applies through **December 31, 2027, 11:59 p.m. Eastern standard time**. From **January 1, 2028, 12:01 a.m.**, clause (3)(a) sends Annex I-C products to the rates in clause (3) of 11021. On the stipulated Canadian, predominantly non-U.S.-metal facts, that is the full-value 25% rate:
- $200,000 × 25% = **$50,000** per unit, absent a subsequent change.
Q13.basis: Proclamation 11032, clause (2)(a)–(d), FR Doc. 2026-11314, 91 FR 34087; clause (3)(a)–(b) and clause (4), 91 FR 34088. Clause (2)(d) originally defines non-U.S. content by subtracting value attributable to parts produced in the United States and establishes the 15% floor. Commerce guidance, FR Doc. 2026-20938, DATES and guidance items 1–2, 91 FR 65162, effective October 14, 2026 at 12:01 a.m., additionally recognizes U.S.-melted/poured steel, U.S.-smelted/cast aluminum, and U.S.-smelted/cast copper to the extent not otherwise counted. Post-2027 rates: 11021, clause (3)(a)–(c), FR Doc. 2026-06960, 91 FR 18204. Most metal being non-U.S. by weight prevents the 85%-U.S.-metal treatment under 11032 clause (4).
Q13.uncertainty: For (f), the later guidance is expressly prospective. No earlier readable guidance authorizing the extra $30,000 metal-value subtraction was located. The calculations treat the stipulated U.S.-produced parts as qualifying parts under the proclamation and guidance; their production facts are not independently audited.

Q14.answer:
(a) Statement 1 — **Partly correct, but incorrect as a hard deadline.** The memorandum's introductory explanation says USTR reported that establishing TRQs would be feasible by September 1. Operative section 2(a)–(b), however, directs establishment “as soon as” USTR determines it feasible; section 2(c) preserves the 10% duty until establishment. The adopted notice likewise says “when feasible” and anticipates a later notice. [FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47720–21; FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47321, 47334–35.]

(b) Statement 2 — **Incorrect for comments on the proposed action.** The June notice reports over 450 comments and nearly 60 witnesses for the earlier actionability proceedings. For the proposed-action phase, the July memorandum and notice report over 1,600 comments and over 100 witnesses at the July 7–9 hearings. [FR Doc. 2026-11296, section I, 91 FR 34273; FR Doc. 2026-15181, sections I and III, 91 FR 47319, 47328; FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47719.]

(c) Statement 3 — **Incorrect.** Six economies adopted prohibitions after June—Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, and Trinidad and Tobago—and Jordan undertook an ART commitment. Cambodia and Guatemala were already proposed at 10%. Thus five nominal rates moved from 12.5% to 10%: Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago, and Jordan; Jordan's stated reason was a commitment, not an enacted ban. [FR Doc. 2026-11296, IV, 91 FR 34274; FR Doc. 2026-15181, I, 91 FR 47319, and II.B.9, 20, 22, 24, 29, 50, 54, 91 FR 47322–24, 47327.]

(d) Statement 4 — **Incorrect.** Commenters sought removal of beef, avocados and other products from exemptions. USTR expressly declined to remove them, citing remaining limited domestic availability. The forced-labor linkage claims were commenters' arguments, not an adopted finding that compelled their removal. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.C.3, 91 FR 47330–31.]

(e) Statement 5 — **Incorrect.** MFN-net economies are EU, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and Switzerland. The readable economy-specific exemption provisions include EU, Switzerland and Taiwan, but no corresponding negotiated product list for Japan or South Korea; their individual determinations refer to the common Part A list. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, II.A, 91 FR 47320–21; II.B.28 and 49, 91 FR 47324, 47327; note 52(j), 91 FR 47363–94.]

(f) Statement 6 — **Partly correct.** USTR states that it exempted an additional 471 products; that is its reported number of additions, not an independently verified net count after cutbacks. It says **certain** sugar and sugar-containing products, not all; the related comments concern in-quota imports. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.D, 91 FR 47331–33.]

(g) Statement 7 — **Incorrect as a claim about total duties.** USTR refers to “maximum tariffs of 12.5 percent” in its response to disruption arguments. In context these are this action's additional tariffs. Note 52(a) makes ordinary and other additional duties cumulative unless an exception applies. Even the MFN-net rules do not reduce an MFN rate already above the threshold. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.E, 91 FR 47334; note 52(a), 91 FR 47352; FR Doc. 2026-15274, section 1(a)(ii), 91 FR 47720.]

(h) Statement 8 — **Correct for goods subject to this additional duty.** The adopted notice expressly requires privileged foreign status for such zone admissions from the date the duty is imposed, except products eligible for domestic status. It is not a rule for every unrelated good admitted to a zone. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, II.A, 91 FR 47321.]

(i) Statement 9 — **Correct, subject to the scope of the judgment.** The memorandum and notice expressly preserve other exemptions/actions and apply the relevant tariff to imports covered by an invalidated exemption or part of one. [FR Doc. 2026-15274, section 4(e), 91 FR 47723; FR Doc. 2026-15181, IV, 91 FR 47335.]

(j) Statement 10 — **Partly correct as a report of USTR's explanation, but not a complete description of the adopted readable framework.** Section III.C indeed says the only products cut back from Annex A were non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemicals. But June's readable Annex A also states blanket exemptions for section 232 goods, informational materials, donations and accompanied baggage, and refers to USMCA-compliant goods. The adopted note instead uses enumerated section 232 headings, personal-use baggage, and goods actually entered free under USMCA, without stand-alone blanket informational-materials/donations exemptions. Thus the notice's chemicals-only account and its operative note do not fully match. [FR Doc. 2026-11296, Annex A, 91 FR 34276; FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.C, 91 FR 47330, and note 52(a), (f)–(h), 91 FR 47352, 47362–63.]
Q14.basis: Citations accompanying each statement identify whether the deciding passage is an operative memorandum section or tariff note, USTR's adopted determination/explanation, a description of comments, or the earlier proposal. In particular, the September 1 statement is introductory explanation rather than an operative deadline; the 471 figure and chemicals-only characterization are agency explanations, not independently readable image-table counts.
Q14.uncertainty: Image product lists cannot be counted or compared independently. Statement 10's product-by-product accuracy therefore cannot be fully audited, but the readable general exemption differences can be established. The invalidation provisions do not resolve every possible judgment's temporal or remedial scope.

Q2.answer:
(a) Section 338 duty:
- Entry 1, August 20 at 2:00 p.m.: $40,000 × 0% = **$0**.
- Entry 2, August 21 at 11:59 p.m.: $40,000 × 0% = **$0**.
- Entry 3, August 22 at 12:01 a.m.: $40,000 × 50% = **$20,000**.
The controlling replacement start is August 22 at 12:01 a.m., inclusive, under Proclamation 11056, clause (1), FR Doc. 2026-17294, 91 FR 54790.

(b) Clause (1) of 11056 first declares that the effective date of the duties in all three original proclamations “shall be” August 22 at 12:01 a.m. It then expressly amends the **chapeau of Annex II** of each original proclamation, replacing “August 19, 2026” with “August 22, 2026.” It does not expressly rewrite the August 19 language printed in clauses (1) and (3) of 11046 or its recital 9. The new substantive effective-date command, together with 11056's clause (5) superseding inconsistent earlier provisions, resolves the difference in favor of August 22.

(c) The excess deposit was $40,000 × 50% = **$20,000**. Clause (4) of 11056 says that, to the extent implementation requires refunds, they “shall be processed pursuant to applicable law and CBP's standard procedures.” It does not identify a particular filing, deadline, or automatic-payment mechanism.

(d) **No further presidential activation was required.** Clause (1) of 11056 sets an unconditional replacement date. Later recitals state that Canada expressed a commitment to remove the discrimination, reneged and ceased good-faith negotiations on August 21, and that the suspension lapsed and duties became effective at 12:01 a.m. on August 22. Those later recitals report what happened; they are not a new activation clause.

(e) The original proclamation describes a minimum 30-day waiting period after the President's discrimination-finding proclamation. It was signed July 20:
- July 20 to July 31 = 11 days.
- July 31 to August 19 = 19 days.
- 11 + 19 = **30 days**.
Thus the original August 19 date corresponds to 30 calendar days after signing, not 30 days after the July 23 publication.

Q3.answer:
(a) The ban turns on **importation**, whereas the tariff ordinarily turns on consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal.
- **A:** May be imported. It arrives and is entered before the ban. Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
- **B:** May be imported. Its September 27 importation is grandfathered even though warehouse withdrawal occurs October 5. Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
- **C:** May be imported. Its September 28, 11:30 p.m. importation precedes the September 29, 12:01 a.m. cutoff; the following morning's entry does not defeat the savings clause. Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
- **D:** Importation is prohibited. Arrival at 12:30 a.m. on September 29 is after the cutoff. There is **no lawful consumption entry under these facts**; paying 50% is not an alternative to the prohibition. No ordinary section 338 duty total can be assigned to a permitted entry.

(b) **E:** The most defensible reading is that the September 25 importation is grandfathered by clause (2) of 11061. It remains subject to the tariff on October 6, not to the ban:
- Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
The original duty proclamation also requires privileged foreign status for covered zone admissions after its effective date, unless domestic status is available. The exclusion proclamation does not expressly discuss zones, but its savings language covers products “imported, but not yet entered for consumption.”

(c) Clause (9)(b) supplies a **50% tariff fallback** if the ban is invalidated as to an import. The defensible prospective treatment for this beer after an applicable invalidation is the restored/original 50% duty, rather than duty-free access:
- Section 338 on a $30,000 shipment: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
The precise effect of a particular judgment would depend on its scope; the proclamation's wording does not itself resolve every temporal question about invalidation.

(d) **No.** Clause (3) says the exclusion proclamation does not otherwise affect the tariff-covered products, apart from changing its Annex products to import-ban treatment. Products outside the exclusion Annex retain their applicable tariff treatment under 11046 as modified by 11064.
Q3.basis: Proclamation 11061, clause (1) (importation cutoff), clause (2) (pre-ban imports retain 50%), clause (3) (other tariff scope unchanged), and clause (9)(b) (invalidation fallback), FR Doc. 2026-18835, 91 FR 58312–13. Original tariff and zone rule: Proclamation 11046, clauses (1), (3), and (4), FR Doc. 2026-14991, 91 FR 46641; replacement effective date: Proclamation 11056, clause (1), FR Doc. 2026-17294, 91 FR 54790.

Q7.answer:
(a) France:
- Column 1-General duty: 2,000 kg × $0.03/kg = $60.
- Ad valorem equivalent: $60 ÷ $12,000 = 0.5%.
- Section 301: $12,000 × (10% − 0.5%) = **$1,140**.

(b) Compound-rate calculation common to all three origins:
- Ad valorem component: $20,000 × 4% = $800.
- Specific component: 4,000 kg × $0.25/kg = $1,000.
- Column 1-General duty: $800 + $1,000 = $1,800.
- Ad valorem equivalent: $1,800 ÷ $20,000 = 9%.
Then:
- Italy section 301: $20,000 × (10% − 9%) = **$200**.
- Japan section 301: $20,000 × (12.5% − 9%) = **$700**.
- Brazil section 301: $20,000 × 12.5% = **$2,500**. Brazil's additional duty is not net of MFN.

(c) Equivalent MFN rate: $2,200 ÷ $20,000 = 11%.
- Taiwan section 301: $20,000 × 0% = **$0**, because 11% is above its 10% threshold.
- Switzerland section 301: $20,000 × (12.5% − 11%) = **$300**.

(d) The specific/compound-to-ad-valorem conversion is in **U.S. note 52(k)**, inserted by Annex I.A.2 of the adopted notice. Its final two paragraphs expressly state the below-threshold netting results. The zero-additional-duty result at or above the thresholds is expressly stated in the memorandum's **section 1(a)(ii)** and in the adopted notice's rate determinations, rather than in those final two paragraphs of note 52(k).

Q11.answer:
(a) **The memorandum describes June's textile proposal as zero-rated, although June left the reduced rate open.** The July memorandum says USTR proposed a mechanism allowing a volume of textile/apparel imports at a “zero section 301 tariff rate” (FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47719). June actually proposed a “reduced Section 301 tariff rate” and solicited comments on the tariff rate, “if any” (FR Doc. 2026-11296, section IV, 91 FR 34274, and section VI, 91 FR 34275). The July notice itself accurately calls the proposal reduced-rate (FR Doc. 2026-15181, section I, 91 FR 47318). The discrepancy is the historical description, not the later decision to adopt zero-rate TRQs.

(b) **The July notice's chemicals-only retention account is broader than the adopted section 232 exemption.** Section III.C says it exempted all products proposed for exemption in Annex A except non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemicals, and “determined not to remove additional products” (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47330). June's readable Annex A expressly excludes “all articles and parts of articles that are subject to section 232 tariffs” (FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34276). Adopted note 52(a) affirmatively imposes the duty on all covered products except specified exceptions; note 52(f) supplies an enumerated set of headings/categories, not that blanket section 232 rule (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47352, 47362–63). Thus the chemicals-only account does not describe the full narrowing of the readable exemption framework.

(c) **The same chemicals-only account does not preserve June's categorical informational-materials and donations language.** June's Annex A expressly says the proposal “does not cover informational materials, donations” (FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34276). Adoption instead establishes the all-products rule with the enumerated exceptions in note 52(a)–(k); it does not enact those two blanket categories (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47352–94). This is a mismatch with the affirmative retention account in III.C, 91 FR 47330—not a finding that every book or every donation is taxable, since itemized or chapter 98 exceptions may still cover an article.

(d) **Accompanied baggage is narrowed despite the chemicals-only account.** June's Annex A excludes “accompanied baggage” without the later qualifier (FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34276). Adopted note 52(a) excepts “products for personal use included in accompanied baggage of persons arriving in the United States” (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47352), whereas III.C's retention account says the only cutback is non-pharmaceutical chemical applications (91 FR 47330).

(e) **USMCA coverage is described differently in the proposal and the retained-exemptions account.** June's readable Annex A says “USMCA-compliant goods of Canada or Mexico” are outside the proposal (FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34276). Adopted notes 52(g)–(h) require products of Canada or Mexico to be “entered free of duty” under USMCA (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47363). That actual-entry condition is more specific than compliance alone and is another qualification not captured by III.C's chemicals-only retention statement (91 FR 47330).

(f) **MFN-only descriptions do not fully describe the adopted South Korea calculation.** The memorandum directs netting against MFN, and the notice's South Korea determination repeatedly describes the base as MFN (FR Doc. 2026-15274, section 1(a)(ii), 91 FR 47720; FR Doc. 2026-15181, II.B.49, 91 FR 47327). Adopted note 52(k), however, expressly says that for South Korean goods with a properly claimed specific or compound **column 1-Special** rate, the equivalent is calculated using that rate; its netting paragraphs refer to the applicable “column 1 duty rate” (FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47394). The readable operative note therefore supplies a Special-rate qualification not reflected in the MFN-only account.

(g) **The dairy exclusion proclamation cross-refers to a dairy scope proclamation that the published series does not supply.** Clause (3) of 11062 says the tariff scope was “further established” in a September 8 proclamation titled Modifying the Scope ... With Respect to Dairy (FR Doc. 2026-18836, 91 FR 58320). The actual September 8 scope texts are 11064, whose clause (1) modifies **11046/alcohol**, and 11065, whose clause (1) modifies **11048/motor vehicles** (FR Docs. 2026-18838 and 2026-18839, 91 FR 58332, 58340). Neither modifies 11047. The affirmative dairy cross-reference cannot substitute for a dairy scope amendment.

(h) **There is a resolved facial start-date inconsistency in the Canada texts.** The original operative clauses (1) and (3) still print August 19 (FR Docs. 2026-14991, 2026-14992, 2026-14997, 91 FR 46641, 46654–55, 46665). 11056 expressly changes the Annex II chapeaux, not those clauses, while substantively commanding August 22 at 12:01 a.m. and superseding inconsistent earlier provisions (FR Doc. 2026-17294, clauses (1) and (5), 91 FR 54790–91). This is not two equally operative dates: the later command resolves it. Later recitals expressly report the August 22 lapse and commencement (e.g. FR Doc. 2026-18835, recital 4, 91 FR 58311).
Q11.basis: Both sides of each text-level mismatch are cited in the answer. The analysis distinguishes historical descriptions and explanatory retention claims from the operative memorandum sections, proclamation clauses, and adopted tariff note. It does not treat the ordinary June-to-July rate changes, September-to-October reversal of Part A/Part B functions, or publication after an effective date as discrepancies by themselves.
Q11.uncertainty: The chemicals-only retention claim cannot be audited against the image product tables item by item. Items (b)–(e) concern the readable general exemption framework, not an assertion about the treatment of every individual article on an image list. Item (f) establishes a textual qualification; the underlying heading tables are unreadable. Item (g) is an unsupported affirmative cross-reference, not evidence that an unpublished dairy scope change took effect.

Q14.answer:
(a) Statement 1 — **Partly correct, but incorrect as a hard deadline.** The memorandum's introductory explanation says USTR reported that establishing TRQs would be feasible by September 1. Operative section 2(a)–(b), however, directs establishment “as soon as” USTR determines it feasible; section 2(c) preserves the 10% duty until establishment. The adopted notice likewise says “when feasible” and anticipates a later notice. [FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47720–21; FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47321, 47334–35.]

(b) Statement 2 — **Incorrect for comments on the proposed action.** The June notice reports over 450 comments and nearly 60 witnesses for the earlier actionability proceedings. For the proposed-action phase, the July memorandum and notice report over 1,600 comments and over 100 witnesses at the July 7–9 hearings. [FR Doc. 2026-11296, section I, 91 FR 34273; FR Doc. 2026-15181, sections I and III, 91 FR 47319, 47328; FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47719.]

(c) Statement 3 — **Incorrect.** Six economies adopted prohibitions after June—Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, and Trinidad and Tobago—and Jordan undertook an ART commitment. Cambodia and Guatemala were already proposed at 10%. Thus five nominal rates moved from 12.5% to 10%: Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago, and Jordan; Jordan's stated reason was a commitment, not an enacted ban. [FR Doc. 2026-11296, IV, 91 FR 34274; FR Doc. 2026-15181, I, 91 FR 47319, and II.B.9, 20, 22, 24, 29, 50, 54, 91 FR 47322–24, 47327.]

(d) Statement 4 — **Incorrect.** Commenters sought removal of beef, avocados and other products from exemptions. USTR expressly declined to remove them, citing remaining limited domestic availability. The forced-labor linkage claims were commenters' arguments, not an adopted finding that compelled their removal. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.C.3, 91 FR 47330–31.]

(e) Statement 5 — **Incorrect.** MFN-net economies are EU, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and Switzerland. The readable economy-specific exemption provisions include EU, Switzerland and Taiwan, but no corresponding negotiated product list for Japan or South Korea; their individual determinations refer to the common Part A list. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, II.A, 91 FR 47320–21; II.B.28 and 49, 91 FR 47324, 47327; note 52(j), 91 FR 47363–94.]

(f) Statement 6 — **Partly correct.** USTR states that it exempted an additional 471 products; that is its reported number of additions, not an independently verified net count after cutbacks. It says **certain** sugar and sugar-containing products, not all; the related comments concern in-quota imports. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.D, 91 FR 47331–33.]

(g) Statement 7 — **Incorrect as a claim about total duties.** USTR refers to “maximum tariffs of 12.5 percent” in its response to disruption arguments. In context these are this action's additional tariffs. Note 52(a) makes ordinary and other additional duties cumulative unless an exception applies. Even the MFN-net rules do not reduce an MFN rate already above the threshold. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.E, 91 FR 47334; note 52(a), 91 FR 47352; FR Doc. 2026-15274, section 1(a)(ii), 91 FR 47720.]

(h) Statement 8 — **Correct for goods subject to this additional duty.** The adopted notice expressly requires privileged foreign status for such zone admissions from the date the duty is imposed, except products eligible for domestic status. It is not a rule for every unrelated good admitted to a zone. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, II.A, 91 FR 47321.]

(i) Statement 9 — **Correct, subject to the scope of the judgment.** The memorandum and notice expressly preserve other exemptions/actions and apply the relevant tariff to imports covered by an invalidated exemption or part of one. [FR Doc. 2026-15274, section 4(e), 91 FR 47723; FR Doc. 2026-15181, IV, 91 FR 47335.]

(j) Statement 10 — **Partly correct as a report of USTR's explanation, but not a complete description of the adopted readable framework.** Section III.C indeed says the only products cut back from Annex A were non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemicals. But June's readable Annex A also states blanket exemptions for section 232 goods, informational materials, donations and accompanied baggage, and refers to USMCA-compliant goods. The adopted note instead uses enumerated section 232 headings, personal-use baggage, and goods actually entered free under USMCA, without stand-alone blanket informational-materials/donations exemptions. Thus the notice's chemicals-only account and its operative note do not fully match. [FR Doc. 2026-11296, Annex A, 91 FR 34276; FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.C, 91 FR 47330, and note 52(a), (f)–(h), 91 FR 47352, 47362–63.]
Q14.basis: Citations accompanying each statement identify whether the deciding passage is an operative memorandum section or tariff note, USTR's adopted determination/explanation, a description of comments, or the earlier proposal.
